items.title: Night, the clothes on the line
items.body:
The shirts have stopped
their afternoon waving.
They hang now like people
who've finished talking.

I leave them out
one more hour.
Let the night air
have a turn with them.

items.title: Bamboo is a very fast grass
items.body: Bamboo is a grass, and some species are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth: certain kinds have been measured growing close to 90 centimetres in a single day. On a quiet day, you could almost watch it.
items.hook: Wonder: how does a plant grow that fast without collapsing?

items.title: Java 9: Map.of is strict
items.body: Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2) gives a compact, unmodifiable map. It throws if you pass a null key or value, or the same key twice, and its iteration order is not guaranteed. It takes up to ten pairs; for more, use Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(k, v), ...).
items.q: What happens if you pass a null value to Map.of?
items.a: It throws a NullPointerException.

items.title: Books in the running brooks
items.body:
And this our life, exempt from public haunt,
Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks,
Sermons in stones, and good in every thing.
items.who: Shakespeare, As You Like It, Act 2 Scene 1

items.title: The bishop pair
items.body: Two bishops working together cover both colours and sweep across open boards. In open positions they are usually a small but real edge; Larry Kaufman's study of master games valued the pair at about half a pawn. In closed positions with locked pawns, knights often catch up.
items.q: In what kind of position does the bishop pair shine?
items.a: Open positions with clear diagonals.

items.title: Ask for the plan before the code
items.body: Before a bigger change, ask the agent to write a short plan: which files it will touch, in what order, and how it will check the result. Reading a plan takes a minute; untangling a wrong turn takes much longer. Approve the plan, then let it work.
items.q: What should an agent produce before a large change?
items.a: A short plan: files, order and how it will verify the work.

items.title: Logo and the turtle
items.body: In 1967 Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon created Logo, a programming language meant for children. Its famous 'turtle' — first a small robot on the floor, later a cursor on screen — drew lines as kids typed commands like FORWARD 50 and RIGHT 90, turning geometry into something you could steer.
items.q: What did children steer in Logo?
items.a: A 'turtle' that drew lines as it moved.

items.title: The spotlight effect
items.body: In a 2000 study, Thomas Gilovich and colleagues had students walk into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt. The wearers guessed that about half the room noticed; in fact only about a quarter did. We tend to overestimate how much others watch us, which is a gentle reason to worry less about small slips.
items.hook: Wonder: who noticed your last small mistake — besides you?

items.title: Saturn is lighter than water
items.body: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre, less than water's 1.0. So, the old joke goes, it would float in a big enough bathtub. In reality it's a ball of mostly hydrogen and helium with no surface to float on, but the number is real.
items.q: Which planet's average density is less than water's?
items.a: Saturn, at about 0.69 g/cm³.

items.title: Let yourself move while you think
items.body: A 2015 study of children with ADHD found that those who moved more during a working-memory task tended to do better on it. Movement isn't always a distraction; for some brains it helps. A fidget, a standing desk or pacing during a phone call can be a tool, not a fault.

items.title: The cat in Arjuna's Penance
items.body: At Mamallapuram, Pallava sculptors of the 7th century carved a vast relief across two giant boulders, with a natural cleft down the middle that may once have carried water like a river. Gods, people, elephants and a sage in penance fill the rock. Look closely and you'll find a cat standing on its hind legs, copying the sage, with mice gathered round it. Scholars still debate whether the scene shows Arjuna's penance or the descent of the Ganga.
items.hook: Wonder: why would sculptors tuck a joke into a sacred scene?

items.title: Let the scene turn
items.body: A useful check for any scene: is something different at the end than at the start? A hope rises or falls, a secret moves from one person to another, a door that was open closes. If nothing turns, the scene may be a pause rather than a scene — fine sometimes, but worth knowing.
items.q: What's a quick test of whether a scene is working?
items.a: Check that something has changed between its start and its end.

items.title: OpenAI uses its models to help design chips
items.body: OpenAI says its models have been helping improve the design of its own chips. In one case, an AI-suggested redesign of a multiplier shrank its estimated area by about 15% and cut a calculation from two clock cycles to one. It is also working with Synopsys to bring this into chip-design software.

items.title: Sagas: undo by moving forward
items.body: When one business action spans several services, a saga runs it as a series of local transactions. If a later step fails, earlier steps aren't rolled back; instead each runs a compensating action — refund the payment, release the seat. The idea comes from a 1987 paper by Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem.
items.q: What does a saga use instead of a global rollback?
items.a: Compensating actions that undo each earlier step.

items.title: A shrimp's heart is in its head
items.body: A shrimp's heart sits in its cephalothorax, the fused head-and-chest section at the front of its body. Most of its other vital organs are packed in there too, leaving the tail mostly muscle.
items.hook: Wonder: why might an animal keep nearly everything important at the front?

items.title: Pranav Venkatesh joins an esports team
items.body: Grandmaster Pranav Venkatesh has signed with Revenant XSpark as the team's first chess player and will represent it at Google Play Arena in December. The 20-year-old recently won the World Junior Blitz title in Al Ain with 10.5 out of 13.

items.title: Two stars may be feeding the Milky Way's central black hole
items.body: Astronomers led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics traced a gas stream near Sagittarius A* back to IRS 16SW, a close pair of massive stars whose winds collide and throw off dense clumps. Roughly one Earth's worth of gas reaching the black hole every ten years would be enough to explain its gentle present-day glow.
items.hook: Wonder: how much of the galaxy's centre is shaped by just a few stars?

items.title: The tuner's last note
items.body: The piano tuner finished at six and played one scale to check his work. The girl of the house watched from the doorway, too shy to ask. So he played it again, slower, and then once more with only one finger, leaving the last note for her. She pressed it. It rang true. He packed his tools and said, 'Good. Now it's finished.'

items.title: Simula 67, where classes began
items.body: In Oslo in the 1960s, Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard built Simula to model things like queues and ships. Simula 67 introduced classes, objects and inheritance. Bjarne Stroustrup brought those ideas into C++, and through C++ they shaped Java's classes too.
items.q: Which language first introduced classes and inheritance?
items.a: Simula 67, by Dahl and Nygaard.

items.title: Desirable difficulties
items.body: Psychologist Robert Bjork coined 'desirable difficulties' for practice that feels harder but sticks better: spacing sessions out, testing yourself, mixing problem types. The struggle that makes study feel slow is often the very thing doing the work. If it feels a little effortful, that can be a good sign.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your easiest study habits might be the least effective?

items.title: Two kinds of things
items.body: Some things are up to us and some are not. Up to us are our opinions, our aims, our wishes and our aversions — our own doings. Not up to us are our bodies, our possessions, our reputations — whatever is not our own doing.

items.title: Google Labs tries a product agent called Stitch Loop
items.body: Stitch Loop is an experimental agent from Google Labs that connects to a product's codebase and its live usage metrics. The idea is that after launch it keeps looking for possible improvements and works toward goals you set. It's waitlist-only for now.

items.title: Uttiramerur's names in a pot
items.body: On the walls of a temple in Uttiramerur, near Kanchipuram, inscriptions from the reign of Parantaka Chola I (around 920 CE) describe how the village assembly chose its committee members. Names were written on palm-leaf tickets, put in a pot — the kudavolai — and a young boy drew them out.
items.q: What was the kudavolai?
items.a: The pot of palm-leaf name tickets drawn by a young boy to pick committee members.

items.title: Write it as 'if this, then that'
items.body: Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer calls them implementation intentions: plans phrased as 'If it's 9 pm, then I put my keys on the hook.' Linking the action to a cue means you don't have to remember the plan; the cue does the remembering. Studies across many groups find these simple if-then plans help people follow through.
items.q: What is an implementation intention?
items.a: An if-then plan that ties an action to a specific cue.

items.title: Moon dust printed into interlocking bricks
items.body: University of Arkansas researchers used a laser to fuse simulated lunar soil into small, LEGO-like bricks that click together, with no binder added. The bricks are only a few centimetres across and still weaker and more porous than binder-based versions, but the idea is to build with what the Moon already has.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you build first if every brick came from the ground under your feet?

items.title: Java 16: records for plain data
items.body: record Point(int x, int y) {} gives you a final class with private final fields, a constructor, accessors x() and y(), and sensible equals, hashCode and toString — all from one line. Use records for values that are just data. You can still add a compact constructor to validate inputs.
items.q: What accessor names does record Point(int x, int y) create?
items.a: x() and y() — no 'get' prefix.

items.title: 9z Globant wins a third straight Chess Club Showdown
items.body: Team 9z Globant beat Team Liquid 72–28 in the Chess Club Showdown final, its third title in a row. GMs José Martínez and Faustino Oro led the way, while several of Liquid's stars were busy at the Total Chess event in Budapest.

items.title: The dictionary word that never existed
items.body: The 1934 edition of Webster's New International Dictionary listed 'dord', meaning density. It wasn't a real word: a slip marked 'D or d' (an abbreviation for density) was misread as a single word. An editor noticed in 1939, and 'dord' was quietly removed from later printings.
items.q: How did 'dord' get into the dictionary?
items.a: A slip reading 'D or d' (for density) was misread as one word.

items.title: Friday, the auto ride home
items.body:
The meter ticks in rupees
and the driver hums
something older than both of us.

Shop shutters coming down
like eyelids.
A week folds itself
into the back seat beside me,
and for once
I let it ride.

items.title: Genie 4 arrives in Project Genie
items.body: Google DeepMind has opened Genie 4 to eligible AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie. You describe a world in text, step into it, and can reshape the surroundings with new prompts while you explore. The update also adds an agent that builds worlds for you and a gallery for sharing them.
items.hook: Wonder: what small, quiet place would you build first?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: What does a Java record write for you? What does a saga do instead of rolling back? How did Uttiramerur's assembly pick committee members? Why could Saturn, in theory, float?
items.q: What was the ghost word 'dord' supposed to mean?
items.a: Density — it came from a slip that read 'D or d'.

items.title: Ask the agent to point to its evidence
items.body: When an agent summarises a codebase or a document, ask it to name where each claim came from: a file and line, a page, a link. You won't check every one, but spot-checking two or three tells you quickly whether the summary rests on something real, and the habit nudges the agent to read rather than guess.
items.q: What's a quick way to test an agent's summary?
items.a: Ask it to cite sources, then spot-check a few.

items.title: Morning, the rice measured out
items.body:
Two cups, levelled
with the back of a finger.
Washed until the water
runs almost clear.

No one taught me this
in words. I watched,
and now my hands remember
what the morning needs.

items.title: A clue was once a ball of thread
items.body: 'Clue' comes from 'clew', an old word for a ball of thread or yarn. In the Greek story, Theseus finds his way out of the labyrinth by following Ariadne's thread, so a clew came to mean anything that guides you through a puzzle — and the spelling later shifted to 'clue'.
items.q: What did the old word 'clew' mean?
items.a: A ball of thread or yarn.

items.title: Two connected pawns on the sixth
items.body: Two connected passed pawns that both reach the sixth rank are usually stronger than a lone rook, as long as the rook's king is too far away to help. Whichever pawn the rook attacks, the other steps forward, and one of them promotes. It's a neat case of teamwork beating raw power.
items.q: What usually beats a lone rook if its king is far away?
items.a: Two connected passed pawns on the sixth rank.

items.title: The well in the sand
items.body: Dig a well in sand and the deeper you go, the more water rises. So it is with learning: the more you learn, the more understanding flows.

items.title: Attention residue
items.body: Researcher Sophie Leroy found that when people switch away from an unfinished task, part of their attention stays behind with it — 'attention residue' — and the next task suffers a little. A small fix: before switching, jot one line on where you stopped and what comes next. It lets the old task rest.
items.hook: Wonder: what unfinished thing is quietly holding some of your attention right now?

items.title: Where the word 'bit' came from
items.body: In his 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', Claude Shannon used the word 'bit', short for 'binary digit', as the unit of information — and credited the statistician John Tukey with suggesting it. A single yes-or-no answer carries one bit.
items.q: Who did Shannon credit with coining 'bit'?
items.a: John Tukey.

items.title: 86,400: the number for quick estimates
items.body: A day has 86,400 seconds; call it roughly 100,000 for mental maths. So a million requests a day averages about 10–12 per second, and a billion a day is around 12,000 per second. Then remember traffic is uneven: peak hours often run several times the average, so size for the peak, not the mean.
items.q: About how many requests per second is one million per day?
items.a: Roughly 12 on average.

items.title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
items.body: Earth's orbit is slightly oval, and we pass closest to the Sun in early January (perihelion) and farthest in early July. So the northern winter happens when we're nearest the Sun. Seasons come from Earth's tilt, which changes how high the Sun climbs and how long the days last, not from distance.
items.q: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
items.a: In early January.

items.title: End on an image, not an explanation
items.body: When a scene or story is nearly done, resist the urge to explain what it meant. Close on something the reader can see — a lantern lit, a cup set down, a door left open — and let them do the last step themselves. The meaning lands more softly, and stays longer, when the reader finishes it.
items.hook: Wonder: what image would close your current piece of writing?

items.title: Delhi's iron pillar that hardly rusts
items.body: In the Qutb complex in Delhi stands an iron pillar about seven metres tall and some six tonnes in weight, made in the Gupta period around 1,600 years ago. It has stood in the open ever since with remarkably little rust. Metallurgists found that its iron is rich in phosphorus, which helps a thin, protective film form on the surface.
items.q: What helps the Delhi iron pillar resist rust?
items.a: Phosphorus-rich iron that forms a thin protective surface film.

items.title: Let the agent run the tests
items.body: An agent that can only write code is guessing. One that can also run the tests sees its own mistakes and fixes them in the next step. Before a coding task, make sure the agent knows the one command that checks the work, and ask it to run that command before it says it's done.
items.q: What one thing should a coding agent know before it starts?
items.a: The command that checks its work, such as the test suite.

items.title: Apples are roses' cousins
items.body: Apples belong to the rose family, Rosaceae. So do pears, plums, cherries, apricots, almonds and strawberries. Look closely at an apple blossom and you'll see the family likeness: five petals, like a wild rose.
items.q: Which plant family includes apples, almonds and cherries?
items.a: The rose family, Rosaceae.

items.title: Let the phone live in another room
items.body: Even a silent phone on the desk can tug at attention, because part of you keeps checking whether to check it. For a focused block, put it in another room or a drawer, and set a timer on something else. Research on how much this helps is mixed, so treat it as an experiment: try one block with the phone away and notice how it feels.

items.title: FIDE opens a decade of its data to explore
items.body: FIDE and Salesforce launched 'Chess by the Numbers', a site for browsing more than ten years of FIDE tournament, rating and player data. It has ranking charts, a tab on the share of women in chess, a World Championship history section and a head-to-head view of Gukesh and Sindarov ahead of their title match. One example it highlights: the 1984 Kasparov–Karpov match ran 48 games and was stopped without a result.
items.hook: Wonder: what pattern would you look for first in ten years of ratings?

items.title: Your judgement of it
items.body: If something outside you troubles you, it is not the thing itself that disturbs you but your judgement of it — and that judgement is yours to set aside, now.

items.title: The outbox: save the change and the message together
items.body: A service often needs to update its database and publish an event. Doing them separately risks one succeeding without the other. The transactional outbox pattern writes the event into an 'outbox' table in the same database transaction as the change. A separate relay then reads the outbox and publishes. Consumers should be idempotent, because the relay may deliver a message more than once.
items.q: Why put the event in the same transaction as the data change?
items.a: So both are saved together or neither is.

items.title: FORTRAN, 1957
items.body: In April 1957, IBM shipped the first FORTRAN compiler, built by a team led by John Backus. The name means FORmula TRANslation: scientists could write maths almost as they would on paper, and the compiler turned it into fast machine code. It became the first widely used high-level language, and descendants of it still run weather and physics models today.
items.q: What does FORTRAN stand for?
items.a: FORmula TRANslation.

items.title: Why stars twinkle and planets mostly don't
items.body: Stars are so far away that each is a single point of light. Moving pockets of air bend that thin beam this way and that, so the star seems to flicker. A planet shows a tiny disc instead, made of many points, and their wobbles average out — which is why planets usually shine with a steadier light.
items.q: Why does a planet's light twinkle less than a star's?
items.a: It shows a small disc, so the air's wobbles average out.

items.title: Dual coding: words plus a picture
items.body: Psychologist Allan Paivio proposed that we store ideas in two linked forms, verbal and visual. Pairing a definition with a simple sketch, diagram or timeline gives memory two routes back to the same idea. The picture doesn't need to be pretty; a box-and-arrow drawing you made yourself works well.
items.hook: Wonder: which idea from this week could you redraw as a tiny diagram?

items.title: The ferryman's lantern
items.body:
Every evening the ferryman lit his lantern before the last crossing, though the river was short and he knew it blind. A boy once asked why.

'It isn't for me,' he said. 'It's for whoever is waiting on the far bank. They see the light leave, and they know to put their shoes on.'

The boy grew up and moved to the city. Years later, in an office far from any river, he started sending a short message before each meeting: On my way.

items.title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
items.body: Hummingbirds can hover in place and even fly backwards. Their wings swivel at the shoulder and trace a sideways figure-of-eight, producing lift on both the forward and the back stroke — closer to how an insect flies than most birds.
items.q: What lets hummingbirds hover and fly backwards?
items.a: Wings that swivel at the shoulder and make lift on both strokes.

items.title: Checkpoint before you let the agent loose
items.body: Before a coding agent starts editing, make a checkpoint: commit your work or copy the folder. Then every change it makes is a clean diff against something you trust, and if it wanders off you can roll back in one step instead of untangling edits by hand. A safe 'undo' makes it easier to let the agent try bolder ideas.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you let an agent attempt if undo were free?

items.title: Arikamedu, Rome's trading post near Puducherry
items.body: Just south of Puducherry, on the Ariyankuppam river, lies Arikamedu, a port that traded with the Roman world around two thousand years ago. Excavations, including Mortimer Wheeler's in 1945, turned up Roman wine jars (amphorae) and fine red Arretine pottery from Italy, alongside local bead-making. It's a quiet riverside spot that once linked Tamil country to the Mediterranean.
items.q: What Roman goods were found at Arikamedu?
items.a: Amphorae (wine jars) and Arretine pottery.

items.title: Give the task a time, not just a place on the list
items.body: A to-do list says what; a calendar says when. Pick one task and put it in your calendar as a real appointment — '10:30–11:00, draft the email' — with a start time you'll actually see. When the slot arrives, the decision is already made, and you only have to begin. If it slips, just drag it to the next free slot; no penalty.

items.title: Java: orElse vs orElseGet
items.body: optional.orElse(makeDefault()) always calls makeDefault(), even when the Optional has a value — Java evaluates arguments before the call. optional.orElseGet(this::makeDefault) only runs it when the Optional is empty. For a constant, orElse is fine; for anything costly or with side effects, use orElseGet.
items.q: When does orElse evaluate its argument?
items.a: Always, even if the Optional holds a value.

items.title: Checking a tiny twist in the oldest light
items.body: Some measurements hint that the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, the universe's oldest light, may be rotated by a small angle, roughly a third of a degree. If real, that could point to new physics. A UC San Diego team (Lonappan, Keating and Arnold) has a new way to check: compare maps made by different groups of detectors in Planck data, so a misaligned instrument can't fake the signal. The work doesn't confirm the twist; it makes the test sharper.
items.q: Why compare maps from different detector groups?
items.a: To rule out an instrument misalignment that could mimic the rotation.

items.title: Giri takes the lead in the Total Chess final
items.body: In Budapest, Anish Giri won the first day of the Total Chess final against Alireza Firouzja, 11–9. They shared the rapid games and drew the fast classical game, so blitz decided the day. A win or a draw on Friday would give Giri the title without a tiebreak. In the third-place match, Fabiano Caruana leads Maxime Vachier-Lagrave 11–9.
items.hook: Wonder: in a mixed-format match, which speed of chess shows a player's real strength?

items.title: Friday, the first light on the stairs
items.body:
Light comes up the stairs
before anyone does,
one step at a time,
as if it, too, were careful not to wake us.

By the landing it has warmed
the banister.
By the top it is morning,
and the week is nearly done.

items.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon
items.body: Google released Gemini 4 Neon on 18 November. It takes up to a million tokens of context and is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, available through Google's API and to eligible Gemini subscribers.
items.q: How large is Gemini 4 Neon's context window?
items.a: About one million tokens.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: What does orElse do that orElseGet doesn't? Why do stars twinkle while planets mostly shine steadily? Which port near Puducherry traded with Rome? What does attention residue mean?
items.q: Roughly how many seconds are in a day?
items.a: 86,400 — handy for turning daily counts into per-second rates.

items.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion adds models and more places to run
items.body: GitHub updated Copilot Fusion, which routes work across several models. It now includes Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Terra and Microsoft's MAI-Code-2 at different tiers, and is available in the web app, Visual Studio, and a mobile beta. GitHub reports a 71.2% score on the public Terminal-Bench 4.1 leaderboard.
items.q: What does Copilot Fusion do with multiple models?
items.a: It routes tasks across them at different tiers.

items.title: Night, the kettle cooling
items.body:
The kettle ticks as it cools,
a small clock running down.

The last cup is drunk.
The spoon rests on its saucer like an oar.

Nothing left to boil,
nothing left to fix —
the house breathes out.

items.title: Leases: a lock that expires
items.body: In a distributed system, a node holding a lock might crash and never release it. A lease fixes this: the lock is granted for, say, ten seconds, and the holder must renew it to keep it. If the holder goes quiet, the lease simply runs out and someone else can take over. Pair it with a fencing token so a slow old holder can't overwrite the new one.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your 'forever' locks would be safer with an expiry date?

items.title: Spacewar!, 1962
items.body: In 1962, Steve Russell and friends at MIT wrote Spacewar! for the PDP-1: two spaceships duelling around a star whose gravity pulled them in. It was one of the first video games, and copies spread to other labs on paper tape — a playful early sign that computers could be for fun too.
items.q: Which computer was Spacewar! written for?
items.a: The DEC PDP-1.

items.title: Ripe fruit at hand
items.body: To speak harsh words when kind ones are at hand is like reaching for unripe fruit while the ripe hangs within reach.

items.title: The gegenschein, the counter-glow
items.body: On a very dark night, the point in the sky directly opposite the Sun can show a faint, oval patch of light: the gegenschein (German for 'counter-shine'). It's sunlight bouncing straight back off dust in the plane of the planets, just as a field looks brightest when the Sun is behind you.
items.q: Where in the sky is the gegenschein?
items.a: Directly opposite the Sun.

items.title: The pre-mortem
items.body: Before starting a project, imagine it's six months later and it went badly. Now list the reasons why. Psychologist Gary Klein proposed this 'pre-mortem': because the failure is presented as already happened, people find it easier to name risks they'd otherwise keep quiet about. It's planning with hindsight you borrowed early.
items.q: What's the key twist of a pre-mortem?
items.a: You imagine the failure has already happened, then explain why.

items.title: World Junior Championship opens in Caracas
items.body: The World Junior U20 Championship began in Caracas, Venezuela, with 136 players from 32 countries in Open and Girls sections. Each section is an 11-round Swiss with classical time controls, running until 27 November — a long, thoughtful event for the game's rising players.
items.hook: Wonder: how does a nine-day classical event feel different from a single blitz evening?

items.title: Koalas have fingerprints
items.body: Koalas have fingerprints with loops and whorls so similar to ours that they're hard to tell apart even under a microscope. It's a lovely case of convergent evolution: both species grip things with their hands, and ridged skin helps.
items.q: Which marsupial has fingerprints that closely resemble human ones?
items.a: The koala.

items.title: Give the agent a budget
items.body: An agent with no limits can wander. Give it a clear allowance — say, twenty tool calls or ten minutes — and ask it to report what it found when the budget runs out. A budget turns an open-ended hunt into a scoped task, and the summary at the end is often the most useful part.
items.hook: Wonder: what budget would you give yourself for the same task?

items.title: Kailasanathar, Kanchipuram's sandstone temple
items.body: The Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram was built around 700 CE under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha. It is among the earliest structural (built, not rock-cut) temples in South India, and its small shrines around the courtyard still carry traces of old paintings.
items.q: Which dynasty built the Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram?
items.a: The Pallavas (under Narasimhavarman II, Rajasimha).

items.title: The tailor's chalk
items.body:
The tailor kept a stub of chalk no longer than a fingernail. Customers offered to buy him a new box. He only smiled.

One evening his apprentice asked why. The tailor drew a single line across blue cloth, thin and sure. 'A new piece is bold,' he said. 'It wants to be seen. This one has learned to say only what is needed.'

The apprentice pocketed the next worn stub before it could be thrown away.

items.title: Bundle the dull with the pleasant
items.body: Pair a task you avoid with something you enjoy that you only allow during it — a favourite podcast only while folding laundry, a special tea only while doing paperwork. Researcher Katy Milkman calls this 'temptation bundling', and in her gym study it nudged people to show up more often.
items.q: What is temptation bundling?
items.a: Allowing yourself a treat only while doing a task you tend to avoid.

items.title: Java 17: sealed classes
items.body: A sealed class names exactly which classes may extend it: `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}`. The compiler then knows the full family, so a switch over Shape can be checked for completeness without a default branch. It turns 'I hope nobody adds a subclass' into a rule.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your interfaces really has a fixed, known set of implementations?

items.title: Opposite-coloured bishops: the drawish pair
items.body: When each side has one bishop and they run on different colours, the defender can often build a blockade on squares the attacker's bishop can never touch. Even a pawn or two down, many such endings are drawn. But add queens or rooks and the same imbalance helps the attacker, because the defender's bishop can't guard what the attacker's bishop hits.
items.q: Why are pure opposite-coloured bishop endings often drawn?
items.a: The defender blockades on squares the enemy bishop can't control.

items.title: Linux began as 'just a hobby'
items.body: On 25 August 1991, a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds posted to a Usenet group that he was writing a free operating system for 386 PCs — a hobby, he said, nothing big or professional. That modest note grew into the kernel that now runs most servers, Android phones and supercomputers.
items.q: In what year did Torvalds announce the project that became Linux?

items.title: Mars helicopter blades go supersonic
items.body: NASA engineers spun test rotor blades for future Mars helicopters past the speed of sound. Mars's air is so thin that lift is hard to come by; faster-tipped blades could give roughly 30% more lift, opening the door to bigger, more capable flying explorers on the Red Planet.
items.q: Why is flying on Mars hard?
items.a: Its atmosphere is very thin — about 1% as dense as Earth's — so blades get little lift.

items.title: Let them talk around it
items.body: People rarely say the important thing directly. Two siblings arguing about who should keep a teapot may really be talking about their mother. Let the dialogue circle the subject while the reader quietly notices the centre. What's left unsaid often carries the scene.
items.hook: Wonder: what is your character avoiding saying in their last line?

items.title: The doorway effect
items.body: Walked into a room and forgotten why? Experiments by Gabriel Radvansky and colleagues found that passing through a doorway makes people slightly worse at recalling what they were carrying in mind — the brain seems to treat the doorway as an 'event boundary' and file the previous scene away. Saying the purpose aloud before you go helps it travel with you.
items.hook: Wonder: what other 'doorways' — a new tab, a new app — might close a mental scene?

items.title: Mistral's Vibe coding agent gets a desktop app
items.body: Mistral released a desktop app for Vibe, its coding agent, on macOS and Windows, with Linux planned. It can run the agent locally or in a cloud sandbox, uses Git worktrees so several tasks can proceed side by side, and plugs into VS Code, JetBrains and Zed.
items.q: What Git feature lets Vibe run parallel tasks without them colliding?
items.a: Git worktrees.

items.title: What our thoughts make it
items.body: The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it.

items.title: A day on Venus outlasts its year
items.body: Venus spins very slowly — and backwards compared with most planets. One full turn takes about 243 Earth days, while one trip around the Sun takes about 225. So a Venusian day (one rotation) is longer than its year.
items.q: Which is longer on Venus: one rotation or one orbit?
items.a: One rotation (~243 Earth days vs ~225 for the orbit).

items.title: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, a capital named for a river
items.body: Around 1025 CE the Chola king Rajendra I founded a new capital and called it Gangaikonda Cholapuram — roughly, 'the town of the Chola who reached the Ganga'. Its great Shiva temple echoes his father's temple at Thanjavur but with gentler, curving lines. It is part of the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples' listing.
items.q: Which Chola king founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram?
items.a: Rajendra Chola I.

items.title: Measure the task in songs
items.body: Minutes are abstract; songs are not. Put on a short playlist and decide the task lasts 'three songs'. You can hear time passing, you know roughly where you are, and the end has a natural signal. Reusing the same playlist can also become a cue that it's work time.
items.hook: Wonder: which task on your list is really only two songs long?

items.title: Vallejo wins the Salamanca Masters
items.body: Paco Vallejo finished the Salamanca Masters with 8.5 out of 10, a point and a half clear of José Martínez. He opened with six straight wins, lost once in round seven, and steadied himself to the end. Loek van Wely took third, and 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan gained valuable experience in a strong field.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a player do the morning after a loss that keeps the next game calm?

items.title: Little's law: queues in one line
items.body: For any steady system, the average number of items inside (L) equals the arrival rate (λ) times the average time each one stays (W). If 200 requests arrive per second and each takes 50 ms, about 10 are in flight at any moment. It needs no assumptions about the shape of traffic, which is why it works for thread pools, checkout lines and kanban boards alike.
items.q: 200 requests/second, 50 ms each — how many in flight on average?

items.title: Webb watches two stars become one in Andromeda
items.body: Astronomers followed a star in the Andromeda galaxy as it swelled into a bloated giant and merged with its smaller companion. Webb's infrared view let them piece together the before, during and after. The single star left behind, nicknamed Bao, may have been given a fresh lease of life by the merger.
items.q: Which neighbouring galaxy hosted this star merger?
items.a: Andromeda.

items.title: Thursday, the night bus
items.body:
The bus hums the same note at every stop,
as if it has one song and likes it.

A man asleep holds his lunch box like a book.
The conductor counts coins without looking.

Outside, the shuttered shops
keep their names lit for no one —
just in case.

items.title: Coding agents now finish more of OpenAI's research chores
items.body: OpenAI published a look at how well coding agents handle its own internal research tasks. On jobs that take a person two to four hours, agents now finish about 46% unaided, up from 23% in March. The progress is uneven — strong on monitoring training runs, weaker on serving code — which OpenAI calls a 'jagged frontier'.
items.hook: Wonder: which parts of your own work are the smooth edge, and which are the jagged one?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: What does Little's law connect? Why do opposite-coloured bishops often draw? Which Chola king built Gangaikonda Cholapuram? Why is a day on Venus longer than its year?
items.q: In Little's law L = λW, what is W?
items.a: The average time each item spends in the system.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: What limits the biggest burst in a token bucket? What does triangulation change? Where is the Roman telescope going? Why is every Chola bronze unique?
items.q: Which method casts the Chola bronzes?
items.a: Lost-wax casting.

items.title: Let the agent wait for you
items.body: Not every step should be done in one sitting. Google's Agent Development Kit can pause an agent, hand back a receipt, and resume hours later when a person approves or replies. Designing agents that can wait patiently — rather than guessing to keep moving — keeps people in charge of the decisions that matter.
items.hook: Wonder: which step in your work would you want an agent to pause before?

items.title: Night, the last light switch
items.body:
One by one the rooms go dark
like pages being turned.

The fan slows into its own sound.
The clock admits it has been talking all day.

I leave the window open a hand's width —
enough for the night
to come in and sit down.

items.title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
items.body: Iron expands when it warms. On hot days the Eiffel Tower stands several centimetres taller than in winter, and its top leans very slightly away from the sun as one side heats faster than the other.
items.q: Why is the Eiffel Tower taller in summer?
items.a: Thermal expansion — the iron lengthens as it warms.

items.title: Gather like the bees
items.body: We should imitate the bees: they wander from flower to flower, choose what suits honey, and then sort and arrange in their combs whatever they have gathered.

items.title: Java: CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly lists
items.body: A plain ArrayList shared between threads needs locking. CopyOnWriteArrayList takes a different deal: every write copies the whole array, and every reader iterates over a snapshot that never changes underneath it — so no ConcurrentModificationException. Great for listener lists that are read constantly and changed rarely; poor for lists that change often.
items.q: Why can't iterating a CopyOnWriteArrayList throw ConcurrentModificationException?
items.a: The iterator walks a snapshot; writes create a new array instead of changing the old one.

items.title: Triangulation: losing a move on purpose
items.body: Sometimes the side to move is the one in trouble. A king can 'waste' a move by walking a small triangle — reaching in three moves a square it could reach in two. The position looks the same, but now it's the opponent's turn, and they must give way. It's one of the purest ideas in king-and-pawn endings.
items.q: What does triangulation change in a position?
items.a: Only whose turn it is — passing the move to the opponent.

items.title: The first website is still there
items.body: Tim Berners-Lee's first website, at info.cern.ch, explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it. It went public in 1991. In 2013 CERN restored it at its original address, so you can still visit the web's first page today.
items.hook: Wonder: what would the first page of your own 'web' have said?

items.title: Review the slip like a scientist
items.body: When something slips — a missed call, a late form — skip the verdict on yourself and ask three curious questions: what was I doing when it slipped, what would have reminded me, and what's the smallest change for next time? You get a fix instead of a bad mood, and fixes add up.

items.title: Dansborg, a Danish fort on the Tamil coast
items.body: At Tharangambadi (Tranquebar) on the Coromandel coast stands Dansborg, a fort built by the Danes in 1620 after an agreement with the Thanjavur Nayak ruler. For over two centuries the town was a Danish trading post. Today the fort is a museum looking out over a calm stretch of sea.
items.q: Which European country built Dansborg at Tharangambadi?
items.a: Denmark, in 1620.

items.title: The conductor's spare coin
items.body: Every evening the conductor on the 21G kept one rupee in his shirt pocket that he never used for change. Students short by a coin would find their ticket punched anyway, the rupee moved quietly from pocket to bag. In twenty years he lost count of the rupees. On his last day, the bag rattled when he handed it in: someone had been slipping coins back in, a few at a time, for years.

items.title: Webb sees jets carving a star nursery
items.body: A Webb near-infrared image of NGC 7129 shows a cloud where stars are being born. Older young stars sit in golden gas on one side; younger ones hide in red, threadlike gas on the other, likely shaped by jets and winds streaming from the newborn stars. Distant galaxies peek through in the background.
items.q: Why does Webb look in infrared to see star birth?
items.a: Infrared light passes through dust that blocks visible light, revealing the young stars inside.

items.title: Thinking longer, choosing no better
items.body: A new preprint tested ten frontier models on shopping-style decisions and found that asking them to reason longer made them more confident but not more often right. It's a useful reminder: extra deliberation helps when there's something to work out, not always when the choice depends on missing information.
items.hook: Wonder: when has 'sleeping on it' helped you — and when did you just need one more fact?

items.title: Sleep files the day away
items.body: Studies of learning and sleep suggest the brain replays and strengthens new memories while we sleep, especially things we practised that day. A good night after studying often helps recall more than an extra late hour of cramming. Learning in the evening and reviewing briefly the next morning is a gentle way to use this.

items.title: A pumpkin is a berry
items.body: Botanically, a berry is a fleshy fruit grown from a single flower's ovary, with seeds inside. By that definition pumpkins, cucumbers and watermelons all count — they're a kind of berry called a pepo, with a tough rind.
items.hook: Wonder: which other 'vegetables' in your kitchen are secretly fruit?

items.title: Java: try-with-resources
items.q: In what order are multiple resources closed?
items.a: Reverse order of declaration — last opened, first closed.

items.title: Enter late, leave early
items.body: Start a scene as close to its turning point as you can, and leave as soon as it has turned. Skip the hellos, the parking, the 'how was your day'. Readers fill in the edges easily; what they want is the moment something shifts. If a scene feels slow, try deleting its first and last few lines.

items.title: The rule of the square
items.body: Can a lone king catch a runaway pawn? Imagine a square whose side runs from the pawn to its promotion square. If the defending king can step inside that square on its move, it catches the pawn; if not, the pawn queens. (Count from the pawn's starting rank carefully if it can still move two squares.)
items.q: What decides whether a king can catch a passed pawn in a pure race?
items.a: Whether the king can step into the pawn's 'square' on its move.

items.title: The right time and place
items.body: Even the whole world can be won, if you act at the right time and in the right place.

items.title: The Milky Way and an aurora, side by side
items.body: This week's Astronomy Picture of the Day shows two glowing arches over Kvaløya in northern Norway. On the left is the band of our galaxy, light that set out thousands of years ago. On the right is an aurora, hours old, glowing about a hundred kilometres up. The Big Dipper and the Andromeda galaxy are tucked into the same frame.
items.hook: Wonder: how can two arches that look the same size be so different in distance?

items.title: Unix began on a spare PDP-7
items.body: In 1969 Ken Thompson at Bell Labs found a little-used DEC PDP-7 and began writing a small operating system on it, joined soon by Dennis Ritchie. One early motivation was to keep running a game he'd written called Space Travel. That modest system grew into Unix, whose ideas live on in Linux, macOS and Android.
items.q: Which machine did Unix first run on?
items.a: A DEC PDP-7 at Bell Labs, in 1969.

items.title: LangChain lets agents wake up on a schedule
items.body: LangChain added a Schedules SDK to its managed Deep Agents, so an agent can run on a timetable instead of only when someone types to it. The idea is 'proactive' agents — for example, tidying a memory store or triaging a queue every morning before you look.
items.hook: Wonder: what's one small job you'd like done before you wake up?

items.title: Chola bronzes, made with wax
items.body: The famous Chola bronzes, like the dancing Nataraja, were cast by the lost-wax method. The artist first sculpts the figure in beeswax, covers it in clay, then heats it so the wax melts away and leaves a hollow mould for the molten metal. Because the mould is broken to free the figure, each piece is one of a kind. Artisans in Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam, still work this way.
items.q: Why is every lost-wax bronze unique?
items.a: The wax model melts away and the clay mould is broken to release the casting, so neither can be reused.

items.title: Keep a 'done' list
items.body: A to-do list only shows what's left. Next to it, jot each thing you finish — even 'replied to Ravi' or 'found the charger'. By evening you have proof the day moved, which makes tomorrow's start easier. Many people with ADHD underestimate what they got done; the list quietly corrects that.

items.title: Butterflies taste with their feet
items.body: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet. When a female lands on a leaf, she can 'taste' whether it's the right plant for her caterpillars before laying eggs.
items.hook: Wonder: what would breakfast be like if you tasted it by standing on it?

items.title: Token bucket: allow bursts, keep the average
items.body: Picture a bucket that holds up to N tokens and refills at a steady rate r. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request waits or is refused. A quiet client saves up tokens and can burst up to N at once, but over time nobody gets more than r per second. It's a simple, memory-light way to be fair without being rigid.
items.q: In a token bucket, what limits the largest burst?
items.a: The bucket's capacity, N.

items.title: Chunking: how masters see the board
items.body: In the 1970s William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess masters a real position for a few seconds; they rebuilt it far better than beginners. With pieces placed at random, the masters' advantage mostly vanished. Experts don't have bigger memories — they store familiar patterns as single 'chunks'. The same is true in code, music and language: learning the common patterns frees your mind for the new part.
items.q: What happened to the masters' memory edge when pieces were placed randomly?
items.a: It largely disappeared — their skill was pattern knowledge, not raw memory.

items.title: Giri and Firouzja reach the Total Chess final
items.body: Anish Giri and Alireza Firouzja will meet in the final of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on 19–20 November. Giri beat Maxime Vachier-Lagrave on both semifinal days without losing a game. Firouzja and Fabiano Caruana split the two days, so it went to a single Armageddon game, which Firouzja won when Caruana's clock ran out.
items.q: In Armageddon, what does Black win with a draw?
items.a: The game — a draw counts as a win for Black, who plays with less time on the clock.

items.title: Thursday, the first tap
items.body:
The tap coughs once,
then remembers it is a river.

I hold the steel pot under it
and wait the way the pot waits —
without a plan, only a shape.

Outside, a crow tries one word
over and over
until the morning agrees.

items.title: Roman's first pictures arrive on 7 December
items.body: NASA will show the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Monday, 7 December, streamed live from the AGU meeting in San Francisco at 3:30 p.m. Eastern (2 a.m. on 8 December in India). Roman launched on 30 August on a Falcon Heavy and is heading for a quiet spot beyond the Moon called L2. NASA is also inviting people to 'adopt' a pixel of that first image.
items.q: Where is the Roman telescope heading to do its work?
items.a: Sun–Earth L2, a stable point about 1.5 million km from Earth on the side away from the Sun.

items.title: KPMG tries an audit with 100 AI agents on the team
items.body: KPMG UK ran an experiment it calls Project Exponential: more than 100 AI agents worked alongside a human audit team on the accounts of a FTSE 250 company over about four months. The firm says the agents sometimes dug into issues more deeply than people did. It wasn't the official audit, and KPMG plans to try the approach on up to 20 larger audits next.
items.hook: Wonder: is a good auditor mostly someone who asks one more question?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: How far from the Sun is 2026 ED138? What does the length of a bee's waggle run tell others? Which language first needed garbage collection? In a king-and-pawn ending, who has the opposition?
items.q: Which of these four could you answer without looking?
items.a: About 46 times Earth's distance. How far away the food is. Lisp. The side not to move.

items.title: Let a fresh session review the work
items.body: An agent that wrote the code is anchored on its own reasoning, much like a person proofreading their own essay. Open a new session with no history, give it only the diff and the goal, and ask it to look for problems. A clean reviewer notices things the author has stopped seeing.
items.q: Why use a fresh session to review an agent's work?
items.a: It isn't anchored on the author's reasoning, so it spots what the author no longer sees.

items.title: Night, the last train announcement
items.body:
The voice on the platform
says the last train's name
as gently as a lullaby.
A few of us stand,
carry our day to the yellow line,
and the doors open
like a room someone kept warm for us.

items.title: Sharks are older than trees
items.body: Sharks appear in the fossil record around 450 million years ago. The first true trees grew roughly 385 million years ago. So for tens of millions of years, sharks swam in seas beside continents without a single forest.
items.hook: Wonder: what did the land look like before any trees?

items.title: Write-ahead logging: note it down before you do it
items.body: Before a database changes its data files, it appends a record of the change to a log and makes sure that log is safely on disk. If the power goes out mid-update, it replays the log on restart and finishes or undoes the work. Appending to one file is fast, and the log becomes the single source of truth for recovery.
items.q: What must be safely on disk before a database applies a change?
items.a: The log record describing that change.

items.title: The opposition
items.body: When the two kings stand on the same line with one square between them, the side that does NOT have to move 'has the opposition'. The other king must step aside and let it through. In king-and-pawn endings, taking the opposition is often the difference between a win and a draw.
items.q: Kings face each other with one square between. Who has the opposition?
items.a: The side that is not to move.

items.title: The work, not the fruit
items.body: Your claim is on the work alone, never on its fruits. Don't let the reward be your reason for acting, and don't let that turn you toward doing nothing.

items.title: Computer time starts on 1 January 1970
items.body: Unix systems keep time as a count of seconds since midnight UTC on 1 January 1970, a date known as the epoch. It was a convenient round starting point in Unix's early years, and it stuck. Ask almost any server for the time and, underneath, it's counting up from that New Year.
items.q: What's the starting moment of Unix time?
items.a: 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970.

items.title: A possible answer to Webb's 'little red dots'
items.body: The James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding compact red objects in the early universe that don't fit neat categories. New computer simulations suggest they could be what remains of enormous primordial stars wrapped in thick gas. It's one strong idea among several, and more observations will help decide.
items.q: What did the new simulations suggest the little red dots might be?
items.a: Remnants of huge primordial stars wrapped in dense gas.

items.title: Plan the next 90 minutes, not the whole day
items.body: A full-day plan can be wrecked by one surprise, and then it's tempting to drop it altogether. A shorter horizon is easier to hold: what are the one or two things for the next 90 minutes? When that block ends, make the next small plan. The day still gets shaped, one piece at a time.

items.title: Athangudi tiles: floors made without a kiln
items.body: In Chettinad, artisans make Athangudi tiles by hand. Coloured cement is poured into a patterned mould set on a sheet of glass, backed with a sand-and-cement mix, then left to dry and cured in water. They're never fired, and the glass gives the face its soft shine. The old Chettinad mansions are known for floors made of them.
items.q: What gives Athangudi tiles their smooth, glossy face?
items.a: They're cast face-down on a sheet of glass.

items.title: Perplexity starts a research group for AI that runs experiments
items.body: Perplexity announced Frontier Research, an effort to build AI systems that propose hypotheses, design experiments and revise their conclusions. It plans to publish its findings, code and models openly.

items.title: Let 'said' disappear
items.body: Readers glide over 'said' almost without seeing it, which is exactly what you want in dialogue. Fancy tags like 'she exclaimed' or 'he retorted' pull attention away from the words themselves. Use 'said', or skip the tag when it's clear who's talking, and let a small action carry the tone instead: 'Fine.' She folded the letter twice.

items.title: Inattentional blindness
items.body: In Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 study, people counting basketball passes in a video often missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the middle of the scene; roughly half didn't see it. Attention is a spotlight, not a floodlight. It's a gentle reason to look again, on purpose, at things you think you've already checked.
items.q: What were viewers doing when many of them missed the gorilla?
items.a: Counting passes between players.

items.title: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn
items.body: Scotland chose a creature that never existed. The unicorn has appeared in Scottish royal heraldry for centuries, standing for purity and strength, and it's often shown chained, a sign of its power being tamed. You can still spot unicorns on old mercat crosses and gateways across Scotland.
items.hook: Wonder: what imaginary animal would you choose to stand for your city?

items.title: Firouzja and Giri win the first semifinal round in Budapest
items.body: At the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot in Budapest, Alireza Firouzja beat Fabiano Caruana 12–8 after building a 4–0 lead in blitz, and Anish Giri beat Maxime Vachier-Lagrave 14.5–5.5. The next semifinal round begins on 18 November; the event runs until 21 November.
items.q: Who did Giri beat in the first semifinal round?
items.a: Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, 14.5–5.5.

items.title: Java: StringBuilder when you build in a loop
items.body: Strings in Java never change, so s += piece inside a loop creates a new String every time and copies everything so far. Over many iterations that adds up. A StringBuilder grows in place: sb.append(piece) in the loop, then sb.toString() once at the end. For a single line like a + b + c, the compiler already handles it; the loop is where it matters.
items.q: Why is s += piece slow inside a long loop?
items.a: Each step makes a new String and copies all the previous text.

items.title: Space dust hints at a hidden store of 'heavy water'
items.body: Researchers at NASA's Johnson Space Center and UCLA studied twelve tiny dust grains collected high in Earth's atmosphere by aircraft. Their water carries extra deuterium, and the team argues it comes from a reservoir of ice beyond Neptune that never mixed with the inner Solar System. The work appears in Science Advances.
items.hook: Wonder: what else is still sealed away in the cold outer edges of the Solar System?

items.title: The cyclist's pump
items.body: The man at the corner fixed punctures for twenty rupees and pumped tyres for free. People asked why he didn't charge for air. 'Air isn't mine,' he said, and went back to his patch and glue. Most of the free-air cyclists came back when they did get a puncture. He never mentioned it. He just slid the tube into his bucket of water and watched for the bubbles.

items.title: Garbage collection was invented for Lisp
items.body: John McCarthy created Lisp in 1958. Because Lisp programs build and discard lists constantly, he needed a way to reclaim memory automatically, and his 1960 paper describes what we now call garbage collection. Every Java object you never free by hand owes something to that idea.
items.q: For which language was garbage collection first devised?
items.a: Lisp, by John McCarthy (described in 1960).

items.title: We learn while we teach
items.body: Men learn while they teach.

items.title: OpenCode Browse lets coding agents use your real browser
items.body: A new tool called OpenCode Browse runs a small server that lets coding agents drive your own Chromium browser, with the tabs, logins and extensions you already have, instead of a blank automated one. Handy for testing a site the way you actually see it; worth pairing with careful permission settings.

items.title: A southern script that sailed east
items.body: The script used by the Pallava kings of Kanchipuram, often called Pallava Grantha, travelled with traders and scholars across the Bay of Bengal. Early inscriptions in Cambodia, Java and other parts of Southeast Asia use letter forms closely related to it, and scripts such as Khmer, Javanese and Balinese descend from that family.
items.q: Which modern scripts trace part of their ancestry to the Pallava script?
items.a: Khmer, Javanese and Balinese, among others.

items.title: Escape 'waiting mode'
items.body: A single appointment at 2 pm can make a whole morning feel unusable: you don't want to start anything in case you miss it. Try setting two alarms, one for 'start getting ready' and one for 'leave now', then let yourself do real work until the first one rings. The alarm holds the time so your head doesn't have to.
items.hook: Wonder: how many hours a week quietly go to waiting mode?

items.title: Bees give directions by dancing
items.body: A honeybee back from good flowers performs a 'waggle dance' on the comb. The angle of the waggle run, measured from straight up, matches the angle between the Sun and the food. The longer the waggle, the farther away it is. Karl von Frisch worked this out and shared a Nobel Prize in 1973.
items.q: In the waggle dance, what does the length of the waggle run tell other bees?
items.a: How far away the food is.

items.title: Consistent hashing: a ring instead of a modulo
items.body: With key % N, adding one server reshuffles almost every key. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on the same circle; each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Add or remove a server and only the keys in its arc move, roughly 1/N of them. Giving each server many 'virtual nodes' on the ring spreads the load more evenly.
items.q: Roughly what fraction of keys move when one server joins a consistent-hash ring of N servers?
items.a: About 1/N.

items.title: The testing effect
items.body: Pulling an idea out of memory strengthens it more than reading it again. In a 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students either reread a passage or practise recalling it. A week later, the recall group remembered noticeably more, even though rereading had felt more productive at the time.
items.q: Which beat rereading after a week in Roediger and Karpicke's study?
items.a: Practising recall (retrieval practice).

items.title: Tabatabaei's six-win finish takes Titled Tuesday
items.body: GM Amin Tabatabaei won the 17 November Titled Tuesday by winning his last six games. He and Hikaru Nakamura both reached 9.5 points, and Tabatabaei took first on tiebreak. It's his second Titled Tuesday title, the first coming in August 2025.
items.q: How did Tabatabaei finish the event?
items.a: With six straight wins, then first place on tiebreak over Nakamura.

items.title: Wednesday, the tea strainer
items.body:
Rinsed and hung on its little nail,
the strainer drips its last brown drops
into the sink, one, then a pause, then one.
It has held back leaves all day
and let only the warm part through.
I'd like to learn that trick.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you strain out of today, and what would you keep?

items.title: Liquid AI's small 'decision' models
items.body: Liquid AI released d1.2 and d1.2-ultra, models built for quick, structured decisions rather than long chats: pulling fields out of documents, locating objects in images, and sorting inputs into categories, across text, images and audio. The company says the ultra version tops a decision-focused leaderboard; independent tests will tell.
items.q: What kind of jobs are Liquid AI's d1.2 models aimed at?
items.a: Structured decisions: document extraction, object localisation and classification.

items.title: A large icy world turns up beyond Neptune
items.body: Matthew Holman spotted a new object, 2026 ED138, in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data in October, and the team then found older images going back to 2016. It sits about 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth and is estimated at roughly 600 to 1,500 km across, the largest such find in about two decades. More observations will tell whether it joins Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake as a dwarf planet.
items.hook: Wonder: how many quiet worlds that size are still waiting out there?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try these from memory before scrolling back: What can a Bloom filter never give? Which moon would a new lander visit? Why is the Thiruvalluvar statue 133 feet tall? What does the Philidor defender do once the pawn reaches the third rank?
items.q: Which of these four could you answer without looking?
items.a: Bloom filter: no false negatives. Callisto. The Kural's 133 chapters. Swing the rook back and check from behind.

items.title: Late tea
items.body:
Steam lifts and leans toward the window,
as if it, too, wants to see the street.
No hurry in the cup.
The spoon rests where I left it,
and the evening sits down beside me
like an old friend who doesn't need to talk.

items.title: A knight on the rim is dim
items.body: A knight in the centre can reach up to eight squares; on the edge, four at most; in a corner, just two. That's why players try to bring knights toward the middle early, and why a knight stranded on the a- or h-file often needs two moves to get back into the game.
items.q: How many squares can a knight in the corner reach?
items.a: Two.

items.title: Bananas are a tiny bit radioactive
items.body: Bananas contain potassium, and a small fraction of all natural potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40. The dose is minuscule, far less than what you get from the natural background around you each day. Your own body carries potassium-40 too.
items.q: Which isotope makes bananas slightly radioactive?
items.a: Potassium-40.

items.title: The lotus and the water
items.body: As high as the water rises, so rises the lotus stem; as high as a person's inner drive, so rises their greatness.

items.title: Circuit breakers: stop knocking on a closed door
items.body: When a downstream service keeps failing, a circuit breaker stops calling it for a while. Closed: calls pass through, failures are counted. Open: calls fail fast, without waiting. Half-open: after a pause, a few trial calls go through; if they succeed, the breaker closes again. The struggling service gets room to recover, and your threads aren't tied up waiting.
items.q: What happens in the half-open state of a circuit breaker?
items.a: A few trial calls are let through; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it.

items.title: Name tasks by their first move
items.body: 'Taxes' sits on a list for weeks. 'Find last year's Form 16 in the blue folder' gets done. Rename a stuck task as the first physical action, starting with a verb, and it stops being a cloud and becomes a step.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the very first physical move of the task you've been avoiding?

items.title: Finding your way round the Moon with shadows
items.body: A new preprint by Ian Down, James McElreath and Manoranjan Majji suggests a spacecraft orbiting the Moon could work out where it is from its own solar-panel power readings: the exact moments it slips into and out of the Moon's shadow reveal its position. The idea could ease demand on NASA's busy Deep Space Network.
items.q: What everyday onboard measurement does the proposed lunar-navigation trick use?
items.a: The solar arrays' power output as the craft enters and leaves eclipse.

items.title: The first mouse was made of wood
items.body: The first computer mouse, built in the 1960s by Douglas Engelbart and Bill English at SRI, was a wooden block with two metal wheels set at right angles and a single button. Engelbart showed it to the world in his 1968 demonstration, along with hypertext and shared-screen editing.
items.hook: Wonder: why two wheels at right angles?

items.title: 133 feet for 133 chapters
items.body: The Thiruvalluvar statue at Kanyakumari, unveiled on 1 January 2000, is 133 feet tall: a 95-foot figure standing on a 38-foot pedestal. The height honours the 133 chapters (adhikarams) of the Thirukkural, and the pedestal's 38 feet echo the 38 chapters of its first book, on virtue (aram).
items.q: Why is the Thiruvalluvar statue 133 feet tall?
items.a: To match the 133 chapters of the Thirukkural.

items.title: Let a room tell you who lives there
items.body: Before you describe a character, describe one corner of their room. A shelf of library books three weeks overdue, a mug washed and turned upside down, a calendar still on last month. Readers will build the person themselves, and they'll trust that person more because they did the work.
items.q: What's a quick way to reveal a character without describing them?
items.a: Show a few specific objects in their space and let the reader infer.

items.title: Google Maps can plan a multi-day trip
items.body: Google Maps' Ask Maps feature can now build multi-day itineraries with live details about each stop, and you can adjust the plan mid-trip. Agent features can also look for appointments and contact local businesses on your behalf.
items.hook: Wonder: which small errand would you happily hand to an agent first?

items.title: Spread it out: the spacing effect
items.body: Studying the same material in several shorter sessions with gaps between them beats one long session, even with the same total time. The gaps let you forget a little, and the effort of recalling it again is what strengthens memory. Try: today, in two days, then next week.
items.hook: Wonder: what did you learn last week that you could gently recall right now?

items.title: Philidor: the third-rank defence
items.body: In a rook-and-pawn versus rook ending, the defending king sits in front of the pawn. Put your rook on your third rank (the sixth from the attacker's side) to keep the enemy king out. The moment the pawn steps onto that rank, swing your rook to the back and check from behind: the king has no shelter left.
items.q: In the Philidor defence, what do you do once the pawn advances to your third rank?
items.a: Move the rook to the far end and give checks from behind.

items.title: A flamboyance of flamingos
items.body: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance. Their pink comes from pigments called carotenoids in the algae and brine shrimp they eat; chicks hatch grey and turn pink over a couple of years.
items.q: Where does a flamingo's pink colour come from?
items.a: Carotenoid pigments in its food, such as algae and brine shrimp.

items.title: Java 14: switch as an expression
items.q: Do arrow-style case labels fall through to the next case?
items.a: No. Each arrow case runs only its own expression or block.

items.title: A fresh supernova, close enough to photograph
items.body: A new Type Ia supernova, the explosion of a white dwarf star, has appeared in a spiral galaxy about 50 million light-years away. That is near by cosmic standards, so professionals have already begun detailed follow-up, and it is bright enough for skilled amateur astrophotographers to capture too.
items.hook: Wonder: what was Earth like when that light set out?

items.title: The umbrella mender's map
items.body: The umbrella mender kept a map of the town with tiny pencil dots: one for every umbrella he had fixed. After forty years the dots made a cloud over the old market, thinning toward the hills. A girl asked what it showed. 'Where people kept walking,' he said, 'even when it rained.'

items.title: Tencent releases Hy4 flash, a fast multimodal model
items.body: Tencent has launched Hy4 flash, a multimodal model with 224 billion total parameters, of which only about 12 billion are active for any one request. It accepts up to a million tokens of context and is priced for high-volume, everyday workflows.
items.q: Why can a 224-billion-parameter model be cheap to run?
items.a: Only about 12 billion parameters are active per request (a mixture-of-experts style design).

items.title: Very little is needed
items.body: Very little is needed to make a happy life; it is all within yourself, in your way of thinking.

items.title: Hedy Lamarr's frequency-hopping patent
items.body: In 1942 the actress Hedy Lamarr and the composer George Antheil received a US patent for 'frequency hopping': switching a radio signal among many channels in a pattern known only to sender and receiver. Antheil's idea for syncing it came from player-piano rolls. The patent wasn't put to use at the time, but frequency hopping is now part of everyday radio technology such as Bluetooth.
items.hook: Wonder: what other inventions began with someone borrowing an idea from music?

items.title: The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram
items.body: The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram stands right at the edge of the Bay of Bengal. It was built in granite blocks in the early 8th century under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha. It is among the earliest structural stone temples in South India, and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.
items.q: Which dynasty built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram?
items.a: The Pallavas, under Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha).

items.title: The generation effect
items.body: Information you produce yourself sticks better than information you just read. In classic experiments (Slamecka and Graf, 1978), people remembered words better when they completed them from a clue (hot: c_ _ _) than when they read the full pair. So before checking an answer, try to produce it, even roughly.
items.q: What is the generation effect?
items.a: We remember information better when we generate it ourselves than when we simply read it.

items.title: Keep a parking lot for stray thoughts
items.body: While you focus, keep a scrap of paper or a note titled 'Parking lot'. When a thought pops up (reply to Ravi, buy batteries, look up that song), write three words and go back. The thought is safe, so your brain can let go of it. Clear the lot at your next break.
items.hook: Wonder: how many of today's 'urgent' thoughts will still feel urgent at your break?

items.title: Giri and Firouzja take first-day leads in Budapest
items.body: The Total Chess semifinals began on 17 November. Anish Giri beat Maxime Vachier-Lagrave 14.5-5.5 on the day, winning the long Fast Classic game with White. Alireza Firouzja swept all four blitz games against Fabiano Caruana and won the day 12-8. Each semifinal runs two days, and the final is set for 19-20 November.
items.hook: Wonder: how would you pace yourself in a match that mixes blitz, rapid and classical games?

items.title: Bloom filters: 'definitely not' or 'maybe'
items.body: A Bloom filter is a small bit array plus a few hash functions. To add an item, set the bits its hashes point to. To check an item, look at those bits: if any is 0, the item was definitely never added; if all are 1, it was probably added. No false negatives, a tunable rate of false positives. Databases use them to skip disk reads for keys that aren't there.
items.q: Can a Bloom filter ever say 'not present' for an item that was added?
items.a: No. It can give false positives, never false negatives.

items.title: Wombats make cube-shaped droppings
items.body: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings. A 2021 study found it comes from the last part of the intestine, where walls of different stiffness press the waste into corners as it dries. Wombats stack them on rocks and logs as scent markers, and cubes don't roll away.
items.q: Why might cube-shaped droppings be handy for a wombat?
items.a: They stay put on rocks and logs, where wombats use them as scent markers.

items.title: A lander for Callisto, Jupiter's quiet moon
items.body: China has outlined plans for a small lander on Callisto, the outermost of Jupiter's four big Galilean moons, carrying two proposed instruments. It would be only the second landing on a Solar System body beyond Mars (the first was Huygens on Titan in 2005). Callisto's ancient surface is among the most heavily cratered in the Solar System, a record of billions of years of gentle bombardment.
items.q: Which of Jupiter's four Galilean moons orbits farthest out?
items.a: Callisto.

items.title: Wednesday, the first bus
items.body:
The first bus sighs at the corner,
empty, lit like a lantern on wheels.
The driver nods to no one in particular.
I nod back. That counts.
The whole day is still folded,
like a letter nobody has opened yet.

items.title: Hugging Face now routes model calls through OpenRouter
items.body: Hugging Face has teamed up with OpenRouter: language-model requests made through Hugging Face can now be routed via OpenRouter, which picks a provider by price, speed and reliability. Developers keep the same Hugging Face token and API, so nothing in their code has to change.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you build if switching model providers cost nothing?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try answering before you peek. Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading does.
items.q: 1) Which numbers did Lovelace's Note G compute? 2) How many years old was Aryabhata when he wrote the Aryabhatiya? 3) In the Lucena position, what do you build?
items.a: 1) Bernoulli numbers. 2) 23. 3) A bridge: the rook goes to the fourth rank to block checks.

items.title: Night, the neem tree
items.body:
The neem keeps a few leaves awake
to talk to the streetlight.
The rest have folded into the dark,
the way a house goes quiet room by room.
I leave the window open a hand's width:
enough for the tree,
enough for me.

items.title: The panda's extra 'thumb'
items.body: A giant panda can grip bamboo with what looks like a sixth finger. It isn't a true thumb: it's an enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid, which acts like a thumb pad the panda presses bamboo against.
items.q: What is a giant panda's 'thumb' really?
items.a: An enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid.

items.body: Learn thoroughly what is worth learning; and having learned it, live by it.
items.hook: Wonder: what did you learn this year that you're now living by?

items.title: Tell the agent what 'done' looks like
items.body: Agents stop either too early or never. Before you hand over a task, write two or three checks that mean it's finished: 'the tests pass', 'the page loads with no console errors', 'the summary is under 200 words'. The agent can then test its own work against them, and you can check the same list in a minute.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the one check that would tell you a task is really done?

items.title: The Lewis chessmen
items.body: In 1831, on the Isle of Lewis in Scotland's Outer Hebrides, a hoard of carved chess pieces turned up, most of them made from walrus ivory in the 12th century, probably in Norway. The rooks are warriors biting their shields, the queens rest their cheeks on their hands. Most are now in the British Museum, the rest in the National Museum of Scotland.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your own carved chess set look like?

items.title: Grace Hopper's nanoseconds
items.body: Rear Admiral Grace Hopper liked to hand out pieces of wire about 30 cm (11.8 inches) long. Each was the distance light travels in a nanosecond, a billionth of a second. She used them to show why signals take time and why smaller, closer components make computers faster.
items.q: Roughly how far does light travel in one nanosecond?
items.a: About 30 cm (just under a foot).

items.title: Request coalescing: one trip for many askers
items.body: When a popular cache entry expires, hundreds of requests may miss at the same moment and all hit the database for the same row. Request coalescing (Go calls it 'singleflight') lets the first request do the fetch while the others wait for its result.
