In Java, a ConcurrentHashMap of in-flight CompletableFutures does the job: the first caller puts the future, the rest join it.
items.q: What problem does request coalescing solve?
items.a: Many simultaneous cache misses for the same key all hitting the backend; only one fetch is made and shared.

items.title: Blue sunsets on Mars
items.body: On Mars, the daytime sky is butterscotch, but sunsets glow blue around the Sun. Fine Martian dust scatters blue light forward, close to the direction of the light source, so the blue gathers around the setting Sun. NASA's Curiosity rover photographed one in 2015.
items.q: What colour is the glow around the Sun at a Martian sunset?
items.a: Blue.

items.title: Stop where it's easy to start
items.body: End a work session just before a clear, easy next step, not at a natural finish. Leave a sentence half-written or the next function named but empty, with a note: 'next: fill this in'. Tomorrow's start is then a small, obvious action instead of a blank page, and getting going is often the hardest part.
items.hook: Wonder: where could you leave today's work slightly unfinished, on purpose?

items.title: Aryabhata's book at twenty-three
items.body: The astronomer Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE, saying he was 23 years old. In compact Sanskrit verse it covers arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy, gives pi as about 3.1416, and suggests that the stars' daily motion comes from Earth turning on its axis. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him.
items.q: What did Aryabhata say causes the stars' daily motion?
items.a: Earth spinning on its axis.

items.title: Guess before you learn
items.body: Trying to answer a question before you've studied the material, even getting it wrong, tends to help you remember the right answer once you see it. Researchers call this the pretesting effect (Richland, Kornell and Kao, 2009). The guess prepares a slot in memory for the answer to land in.
items.q: What's the pretesting effect?
items.a: Attempting questions before studying improves later memory of the answers, even if your guesses were wrong.

items.title: Name the specific thing
items.body: 'Flowers' is a fog; 'jasmine, wilting on the gatepost' is a place. Specific nouns do the describing for you, so you need fewer adjectives. When a sentence feels flat, look for the general word and ask: which one, exactly? A kind of tree, a brand of biscuit, the name of the street.
items.hook: Wonder: which general word in your last message could become a specific one?

items.title: Bland previews a voice model that listens while it talks
items.body: Bland AI has opened a research preview of Tofu-1, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model: it can listen and speak at the same time, with no text transcript in between. Because the audio isn't flattened into words, tone and background sound stay available to the model, which Bland pitches for calls over noisy or weak lines.
items.hook: Wonder: what do we lose when speech becomes a transcript?

items.title: A teaspoon of neutron star
items.body: A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball about 20 km wide. Its matter is so dense that a teaspoonful would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth, more than every car on the planet put together.
items.hook: Wonder: how big would Earth be squeezed to that density?

items.title: Java 21: virtual threads
items.body: Since Java 21 (JEP 444), Thread.ofVirtual() and Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() give you threads that cost little more than an object. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM parks it and frees the underlying carrier thread for others. So plain blocking code can handle many thousands of concurrent requests. Don't pool them; make a new one per task.
items.q: Should you put virtual threads in a pool?
items.a: No. They're cheap; create one per task.

items.title: Lucena: build a bridge
items.body: Rook and pawn against rook, with your pawn on the seventh and your king in front of it, often looks stuck: step out and the enemy rook checks you forever. The fix is the 'bridge'. Bring your rook to the fourth rank, step the king out, and when the checks come, block with your rook. The pawn then promotes. The position carries Lucena's name from a 1497 book, though it actually appears first in Salvio's 1634 work.
items.q: In the Lucena position, which rank does the rook go to for the bridge?
items.a: The fourth rank (from the attacker's side), so it can block checks later.

items.body: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.
items.hook: Wonder: what's today's 'thing', and what's the opinion wrapped around it?

items.title: Pluto's heart
items.body: When New Horizons flew past Pluto in July 2015, it photographed a huge pale heart shape now called Tombaugh Regio, after Clyde Tombaugh, who found Pluto in 1930. The heart's left lobe, Sputnik Planitia, is a smooth basin of frozen nitrogen, slowly churning in cells a few tens of kilometres across, like a very cold, very slow lava lamp.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a nitrogen glacier sound like, if anything?

items.title: Ada Lovelace's Note G
items.body: In 1843 Ada Lovelace translated an Italian article by Luigi Menabrea about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and added her own notes, longer than the article itself. Note G sets out, step by step, how the Engine could calculate Bernoulli numbers. It's often called the first published computer program. She also suggested the Engine might work with symbols, such as musical notes, not just numbers.
items.q: What did Lovelace's Note G show the Analytical Engine computing?
items.a: Bernoulli numbers.

items.title: The cobbler's radio
items.body: The cobbler keeps his radio tuned between two stations, so it plays a little of each and neither wins. A boy asked him once why he didn't fix it. 'Then I'd have to choose,' the cobbler said, and went back to the sole he was stitching, humming a tune that belonged to both.

items.title: Mix it up: interleaving
items.body: Practising one type of problem in a block feels smooth, but mixing types often teaches more. In a 2007 study by Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor, students who practised mixed maths problems did markedly better on a later test than those who practised in blocks. The mix forces you to choose the method, not just apply it, and choosing is the skill the real test asks for.
items.q: Why does interleaving help even though it feels harder?
items.a: It makes you decide which method fits each problem, the skill a real test needs.

items.title: macOS gives users clearer controls over agents
items.body: Apple has described new Mac permission controls coming with macOS 27.3, aimed at apps and AI agents that operate other apps. Permissions are reorganised into clearer groups, there's one consistent way to grant access by picking an app from a list, apps ask per request, and a visible indicator shows when one app is controlling another. Developers get guidance and entitlements for backup and assistive-technology apps.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your apps would you let another app drive?

items.title: Keeladi, a town on the Vaigai
items.body: At Keeladi, near Madurai in Sivaganga district, excavations since 2015 have uncovered an ancient urban settlement: brick structures, drains, ring wells, dice, spindle whorls and many potsherds inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi script. The Tamil Nadu archaeology department's reported dates push some layers centuries earlier than once assumed; scholars are still refining the timeline. A site museum at Keeladi now displays the finds.
items.q: Which river does the Keeladi site lie near?
items.a: The Vaigai, near Madurai.

items.title: Body doubling: work beside someone
items.body: Many people with ADHD find it easier to start and stay on a task when someone else is simply present and also working: a friend at the same table, a colleague on a quiet video call, or an online co-working room. The other person doesn't help with the task. Their presence just makes the room feel like a place where work happens. Research is still early, but it's cheap to try.
items.hook: Wonder: who could you sit quietly beside for 25 minutes this week?

items.title: JP Morgan Chase wins the corporate chess league
items.body: JP Morgan Chase won Season 14 of the North American Corporate Chess League, its first title, beating PwC 3–2 in the final. The top-seeded team also won 3–2 against NVIDIA in the quarterfinal and Susquehanna in the semifinal. FM Maggie Feng clinched the final by winning a tricky endgame. The team was IM Edward Song, FMs Alex Bian and Maggie Feng, NM Asuka Nakamura and Calvin Yang.
items.hook: Wonder: what would your office team's board order be?

items.title: Backpressure: let the slow part set the pace
items.body: When a producer makes work faster than a consumer can handle it, something has to give. Without a plan, queues grow until memory runs out. Backpressure means the consumer signals 'slow down': a bounded queue that blocks or rejects when full, a reactive stream that only sends what was requested, or TCP's window shrinking. The system then runs at the speed of its slowest stage, which is the honest speed anyway.
items.q: What's the simplest way to add backpressure between two threads in Java?
items.a: Use a bounded BlockingQueue (e.g. ArrayBlockingQueue): put() waits when it's full.

items.title: Hera flies in rectangles around Didymos
items.body: ESA's Hera spacecraft has settled in beside the asteroid pair Didymos and Dimorphos, about 25–30 km away, at roughly 196 million km from Earth. Gravity there is so weak that Hera drifts at about 12 cm per second, firing its thrusters every three or four days and turning 90 degrees each time, so its path traces a rectangle. It's set up so that a missed burn makes it drift away, not closer. Next comes a nearer look at about 20 km, and two shoebox-sized CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, will later fly closer still.
items.hook: Wonder: how slowly would you have to walk to match 12 cm per second?

items.title: A strawberry isn't a berry
items.body: Botanically, a berry grows from a single flower's ovary with seeds inside, which is why bananas, tomatoes and grapes count. A strawberry doesn't: its red flesh is a swollen flower base, and each little 'seed' on the outside is really a tiny fruit of its own, called an achene, with a seed inside.
items.q: What are the little 'seeds' on a strawberry's surface, botanically?
items.a: Achenes: each one is a tiny fruit containing a seed.

items.title: Cognition's Devin Bots manage a team of coding agents
items.body: Cognition has introduced Devin Bots, a longer-lived layer that manages groups of its Devin coding agents over days or weeks. A Bot can split a project, such as building an Android version of an iPhone app, into pieces, hand them out, and keep the result in step as the original changes. It joins a team's Slack as a member, remembers context across weeks, and pings people when it needs a decision. Each Bot runs on its own cloud machine with admin-set access to repos and tools, and can have its own budget.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you want a manager-agent to ask you before it starts?

items.title: Tuesday, the stairwell light
items.body:
Press the switch and the stairwell wakes,
keeps its small promise of a minute.
I climb past the shoes outside each door,
the smell of someone's tadka, a radio low.
On the fourth floor the light gives up,
kindly, right as I find my key.

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try answering before you peek. Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading does.
items.q: 1) Which comet feeds the Leonids? 2) What does an idempotency key let a server do? 3) Which dam on the Kaveri is credited to Karikala Chola?
items.a: 1) 55P/Tempel–Tuttle. 2) Return the saved result of a repeated request instead of redoing it. 3) The Kallanai (Grand Anicut).

items.title: Elephants can't jump
items.body: Adult elephants can't get all four feet off the ground at once, even when they move fast. Their 'running' is more of a speedy walk, keeping at least one foot down. With bones built for carrying great weight, they simply don't need to leap.
items.hook: Wonder: which other big animals keep one foot on the ground?

items.title: Key squares: where the king must reach
items.body: In king-and-pawn endings, the attacking king doesn't need to escort the pawn step by step; it needs to reach a key square. For a pawn on e4, the key squares are d6, e6 and f6: two ranks ahead. If the king gets to any of them, the pawn promotes whatever the defender does. (Rook pawns are the exception.) Think of the key squares as the doorway; the king just has to get through it.
items.q: For a white pawn on e4, what are the key squares?
items.a: d6, e6 and f6.

items.title: Give the agent a notes file
items.body: Long tasks overflow an agent's context. A simple fix: ask it to keep a plain notes file in the workspace, recording decisions, what's done and what's next, and to reread it before each step. It costs a few lines, survives restarts, and gives you something readable when you check in.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the one line you'd want the agent to write before it stops for the day?

items.title: Leonids, late
items.body:
I set the alarm for three
and went out with a blanket and no plan.
For a long time, nothing.
Then one thin silver stitch,
the sky mending something I couldn't see,
and gone before I could point.
I stayed another hour
just in case it needed a witness.

items.title: The tongue's burn
items.body: A burn from fire heals in time; a wound made by the tongue does not.

items.title: ENIAC's first programmers
items.body: ENIAC, finished in 1945, had no stored programs; it was 'programmed' by wiring cables and setting switches. The six people who worked out how were Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. They learned the machine from its wiring diagrams, and their work was largely overlooked for decades.
items.q: How was ENIAC programmed at first?
items.a: By plugging cables and setting switches, not by stored software.

items.title: The Pleiades are high on November evenings
items.body: Look east after dark this month for a tiny, misty dipper of stars: the Pleiades, known in Tamil as Karthigai. The cluster is about 440 light-years away and young by star standards, around 100 million years old. Most eyes see six or seven stars; binoculars show dozens, and there are more than a thousand members.
items.hook: Wonder: how many Pleiades can you count before you reach for binoculars?

items.title: Trace IDs: one thread through many services
items.body: When a request passes through ten services, logs alone can't tell you which lines belong together. Distributed tracing gives the request a trace ID at the edge and passes it along in headers; each hop records a span with its own ID, its parent and its timing. Stitch spans together and you see the whole journey, including which hop was slow. The W3C 'traceparent' header is the common standard.
items.hook: Wonder: in your system, which hop would you guess is slowest, and how sure are you?

items.title: An octopus has three hearts
items.body: Two small hearts push blood through the gills; a third pumps it round the body. Their blood is blue, because it carries oxygen on copper-based haemocyanin rather than iron-based haemoglobin. Curiously, the main heart pauses while the octopus swims, one reason they prefer crawling.
items.q: Why is octopus blood blue?
items.a: It carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin.

items.title: Tell the reader where to stand
items.body: Early in a scene, give one concrete detail that places the reader: the smell of the bus depot, the slope of the floor, the light from one window. Readers relax once they know where they are, and then they can pay attention to who is there and what they want.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the single detail that would tell a stranger where you're sitting right now?

items.title: Hampi's stone chariot
items.body: In the courtyard of the Vittala temple at Hampi stands a shrine carved as a chariot, built in the 16th century under the Vijayanagara kings. It houses Garuda, the eagle who carries Vishnu. Its stone wheels were once carved to look as if they could turn, and the chariot now appears on India's ₹50 note.
items.q: Which Indian banknote shows Hampi's stone chariot?
items.a: The ₹50 note.

items.title: The Zeigarnik effect, with an honest footnote
items.body: In the 1920s Bluma Zeigarnik reported that people remembered interrupted tasks better than finished ones. Later studies have been mixed, so it's not a law of the mind. What does hold up is the practical cousin: unfinished tasks tug at attention, and writing down a concrete next step tends to quiet that tug.
items.hook: Wonder: which open loop is tugging at you right now, and what's its next step?

items.title: Mayank Chakraborty wins in Misamis Occidental
items.body: Seventeen-year-old Indian GM Mayank Chakraborty won the Misamis Occidental International Chess Tournament in the Philippines. He led by a full point going into the last round and drew with Vietnam's GM Nguyen Duc Hoa to finish on 7 points from 9, ahead of a 78-player field. Daniel Quizon and Michael Concio Jr shared next place on 6.5.
items.q: How did Mayank secure first place in the final round?
items.a: He drew with GM Nguyen Duc Hoa, keeping his lead to finish on 7/9.

items.title: OpenAI starts a blog about science done with AI
items.body: OpenAI has launched a dedicated science blog to share research results and first-hand accounts from scientists using AI. It plans to cover methods and limitations too, with the aim of making AI-assisted science easier to inspect and reproduce.
items.hook: Wonder: what would make you trust a discovery that an AI helped make?

items.title: Build a launch pad by the door
items.body: Pick one spot near the door, a tray or a hook, where everything for tomorrow lives: keys, badge, charger, the letter to post. Load it the night before, while you still remember. In the morning you aren't searching; you're just picking up.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the one thing you most often walk back inside for?

items.title: Java 12: Collectors.teeing
items.body: Collectors.teeing runs two collectors over one stream and merges their results. For example: stream.collect(Collectors.teeing(Collectors.counting(), Collectors.summingInt(Order::qty), (n, total) -> new Summary(n, total))). One pass, two answers, no second loop.
items.q: How many collectors does Collectors.teeing combine?
items.a: Two, plus a function that merges their results.

items.title: NASA's $1 million Moon Base Challenge for students
items.body: NASA has opened the Moon Base Challenge, a $1 million competition for U.S. high-school and college teams to design pieces of a future lunar base. Teams can work on power, habitats, life support, transport, communications or keeping astronauts protected. Registration runs through NASA's STEM Gateway until 25 January 2027.
items.hook: Wonder: which part of a Moon base would you most want to design?

items.title: The cobbler's spare lace
items.body: The cobbler at the corner kept one black lace hanging from a nail, never for sale. Schoolboys with flapping shoes, a groom ten minutes late, an old man who had tied the same knot for sixty years until it gave: each got the lace, and each came back days later with a new one, sometimes brown, once bright green. He hung whatever came back on the nail. In twenty years he never bought a lace for it. The nail was always full.

items.title: The fruit came before the colour
items.body: In English, 'orange' named the fruit first. The word arrived via French from Sanskrit 'nāraṅga' through Persian and Arabic. Before oranges were common in England, the colour was often just called 'yellow-red'; 'orange' as a colour name only caught on in the 1500s.
items.hook: Wonder: what other colours are named after things?

items.title: The bug that was really a moth
items.body: On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth trapped in a relay and taped it into the logbook with the note 'First actual case of bug being found.' The joke works because engineers had already been calling glitches 'bugs' for decades; Edison used the word in the 1870s. Grace Hopper loved telling the story, and the logbook page now sits in the Smithsonian.
items.q: Where was the famous 1947 moth found?
items.a: In a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer.

items.title: Be the promontory
items.body: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.

items.title: A 145-billion-parameter model for your own computer
items.body: Edge0 has released Edge0-145B, an open-source model built to run on capable personal computers, aimed at coding and harder reasoning. The company says it runs above 80 tokens a second locally with about 29 GB peak memory. A smaller Edge0-120B and local inference tools came alongside. These are the company's own numbers, so expect independent tests to follow.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you ask a strong model if you knew nothing ever left your machine?

items.title: Kallanai, a dam nearly two thousand years old
items.body: The Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, on the Kaveri near Thanjavur is traditionally credited to the Chola king Karikalan, around the 2nd century CE. Built from unhewn stone laid across the riverbed, it diverts water into the delta's canals, and in a rebuilt and strengthened form it still does that job today, which makes it one of the oldest water-regulating works in the world still in use.
items.q: Which river does the Kallanai span?
items.a: The Kaveri (Cauvery).

items.title: The zone of proximal development
items.body: Psychologist Lev Vygotsky described a sweet spot for learning: the things you can't yet do alone, but can do with a little help. Too easy and nothing grows; too hard and help can't reach you. Good teachers, and good tutorials, aim for that middle band, then quietly remove the support as you stop needing it.
items.q: What is Vygotsky's 'zone of proximal development'?
items.a: What a learner can't yet do alone but can do with guidance.

items.title: Nakamura holds off a 15-year-old to reach London
items.body: In the Round of 16 of Speed Chess Championship XI, Hikaru Nakamura beat 15-year-old GM Yagiz Erdogmus 12–8 and booked his place at the live finals in London. Erdogmus made it interesting by winning the bullet segment, the fastest part of the match.
items.hook: Wonder: why might the youngest players shine brightest at the fastest time controls?

items.title: Tuesday, the milk packet
items.body:
Six-ten. The packet on the step
is cold the way only mornings are.
I carry it in like a small moon,
snip the corner, pour,
and the pan begins its slow white thinking.
Nothing is decided yet.
The whole day is still on low flame.

items.title: Idempotency keys: 'I already did that'
items.body: When a client retries a payment or an order because the network hiccuped, the server can't tell a retry from a fresh request. So the client sends a unique idempotency key with each logical request. The server stores the key with the result; if the same key arrives again, it returns the saved result instead of doing the work twice. Keep keys for a sensible window, and store key and outcome in the same transaction.
items.q: What does the server return when it sees an idempotency key it has already processed?
items.a: The stored result of the first request, without repeating the work.

items.title: Make time visible
items.body: Time that you can't see tends to vanish. A visual timer, the kind with a coloured wedge that shrinks, turns 'twenty minutes' into a shape you can glance at without doing sums. Put it in your line of sight, not on your phone, so checking it doesn't open a door to everything else.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your tasks always takes longer than it feels like it does?

items.title: Leonids, after midnight
items.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks around 17–18 November. The Moon is near first quarter, so it sets around midnight, leaving the hours before dawn dark, which is also when Leo, the shower's radiant, climbs high. Expect a gentle 10 to 15 meteors an hour from a dark site. The grit comes from Comet 55P/Tempel–Tuttle, and it meets Earth head-on at about 71 km per second, among the fastest of any shower.
items.q: Which comet leaves the dust behind the Leonids?
items.a: 55P/Tempel–Tuttle, which returns roughly every 33 years.

items.title: Sierra's Poppy: a polite sign on the shop door for agents
items.body: Sierra has released Poppy 1.0, a protocol that lets a business say which actions personal AI agents are allowed to take on its behalf. Shopify has switched it on across its stores, Meta's Muse looks for it automatically, and more than 100 companies are taking part. Think of it as robots.txt for doing things, not just reading things.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you want your own front door to tell a visiting agent?

items.body: digna has launched digna Agentic, digna Data Reconciliation and the digna Engine, tools for checking data quality that can run on-premises, in a private cloud or in a customer's own cloud account. items.title: A banana plant is a giant herb
items.body: The banana 'tree' has no wood. Its trunk is a pseudostem made of tightly wrapped leaf bases, which makes the banana the largest herbaceous flowering plant. After it fruits, that stem dies back and new shoots grow from the underground base to take its place.
items.hook: Wonder: what else in the kitchen garden is not quite what it seems?

items.title: Debounce vs throttle
items.body: Both calm down a noisy stream of events, in different ways. Debounce waits until things go quiet: run the search only after the user stops typing for 300 ms. Throttle sets a steady pace: handle scroll at most once every 100 ms, no matter how many events arrive. Ask: do I want the final value after a burst (debounce), or regular updates during it (throttle)?
items.q: Updating a progress indicator while a user scrolls: debounce or throttle?
items.a: Throttle, for regular updates during the burst.

items.title: Love all, trust a few
items.body: Love all, trust a few, do wrong to none.
items.who: William Shakespeare, All's Well That Ends Well

items.title: You may castle with a rook under attack
items.body: Castling is forbidden if your king is in check, would pass through an attacked square, or would land on one. But the rook has no such rule. It can be attacked, and when castling queenside it may cross b1 (or b8) even if that square is covered. Plenty of club players skip a good castle because they think otherwise.
items.q: In queenside castling, may the rook cross an attacked b1 square?
items.a: Yes. Only the king's start, path and landing squares must be safe.

items.title: Turing's 1936 paper
items.body: In 1936, at 24, Alan Turing published 'On Computable Numbers'. To answer a question in pure logic, he imagined a simple machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape, following a table of rules, and showed that one 'universal' machine could imitate any other. It was a thought experiment, but it's the idea underneath every stored-program computer.
items.q: What could Turing's 'universal machine' do?
items.a: Imitate any other such machine, given its rules on the tape.

items.title: When the alarm rings, stand up first
items.body: A timer goes off and the brain says 'one more minute', and then it's an hour. Make the rule about your body, not your decision: when the alarm rings, stand up. You can sit back down if you truly want to, but standing breaks the spell and gives your brain a moment to choose on purpose.

items.title: Emergency-blanket film for Moon-base insulation
items.body: Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania stacked hundreds of thin Mylar sheets, the shiny film in emergency blankets, into a light insulation they call HyLIFS. Their small samples held up under heavy compression, about 20 MPa, through repeated cycles. That could one day help shelters keep warm through the long lunar night, though the team says making it at scale is still to be worked out.
items.hook: Wonder: what else in a first-aid kit might be quietly space-grade?

items.title: Keep the small promises you make
items.body: Anton Chekhov advised that if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act, it should be used by the last. The principle works for small things too: a locked drawer, a half-finished letter, a recipe nobody can get right. Readers notice what you linger on and quietly wait. Either pay it off, or don't linger.
items.hook: Wonder: what detail in your current draft is quietly making a promise?

items.title: Madras had an observatory in 1786
items.body: In 1786 William Petrie set up a private astronomical observatory in Madras, one of the earliest modern observatories in Asia. A few years later the East India Company took it over, and it was used for star catalogues, timekeeping and mapping India. In 1899 its astronomy work moved up to the clearer skies of Kodaikanal, where a solar observatory still watches the Sun.
items.hook: Wonder: what would the night sky over Madras have looked like in 1786, without city lights?

items.title: Judge your learning later, not right away
items.body: Right after studying something, it feels familiar, so we overrate how well we'll remember it. In a 1991 study, Thomas Nelson and John Dunlosky found that predictions made after a short delay were far more accurate than ones made immediately. So test yourself a bit later, not straight after reading, before deciding what you know.
items.q: When are judgments of 'I know this' most accurate?
items.a: After a delay, not immediately after studying.

items.title: Make an agent's write actions safe to repeat
items.body: A developer-forum bug report this week described an approved tool write running twice when a response continued. Whether or not that bug gets fixed, it's a good reminder: anything an agent does that changes the world (sending, booking, paying, posting) should be idempotent. Give each action a unique key and have the tool ignore a repeat of a key it has already seen.
items.q: What simple guard makes a repeated agent action harmless?
items.a: An idempotency key: a unique ID per action that the tool remembers and refuses to apply twice.

items.title: Rats laugh when tickled
items.body: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that young rats, when tickled, give off rapid high-pitched chirps around 50 kHz, too high for us to hear without special equipment. They chase the tickling hand for more, much like children playing. He described it as a kind of rat laughter.
items.hook: Wonder: how many happy sounds in the world are just out of our hearing range?

items.title: The isolated queen's pawn
items.body: A pawn on d4 (or d5) with no friendly pawns on the c- or e-files is an isolated queen's pawn. In the middlegame it's often a strength: open files for your rooks, a strong outpost on e5, and room for an attack. In the endgame it tends to become a target. So the side with the IQP usually wants action early, and the opponent wants trades, plus a knight parked on the square right in front of it.
items.q: Why does the side facing an IQP usually welcome piece trades?
items.a: The pawn's dynamic strengths fade and it becomes a weak target in the endgame.

items.title: Java 19: HashMap.newHashMap(n)
items.body: new HashMap<>(100) doesn't mean 'room for 100 entries'; it sets the initial capacity, and with the default 0.75 load factor the map resizes after about 75. Since Java 19 you can say what you mean: HashMap.newHashMap(100) sizes the map so 100 mappings fit without resizing. There are matching factories for LinkedHashMap, HashSet, LinkedHashSet and WeakHashMap.
items.q: With default settings, about when does new HashMap<>(100) first resize?
items.a: After roughly 75 entries (capacity × 0.75 load factor).

items.title: The watchman's crossword
items.body: Every night the building watchman did the newspaper crossword, and every morning he left it on the lift ledge with one clue unsolved. For months nobody touched it. Then one Tuesday the gap was filled in, in green ink. The next day, another. He never found out who it was, and he never asked. He just started leaving two clues blank, so they'd both have something to look forward to.

items.title: Why Uranus and Neptune have tilted magnetic fields
items.body: Uranus's magnetic field is tilted about 59 degrees from its spin axis and Neptune's about 47, far more than Earth's. New simulations led by Chi Yan at the University of Texas suggest the reason: electrical conductivity that rises with depth inside these ice giants. The models also predict the magnetic poles could wander noticeably within decades, something future auroral images from Webb might check.
items.q: Roughly how tilted is Uranus's magnetic field from its spin axis?
items.a: About 59 degrees.

items.title: The sweetest music
items.body: 'The flute is sweet, the veena is sweet,' say those who have never heard the babble of their own little ones.

items.title: The Altair 8800 on a magazine cover
items.body: The January 1975 cover of Popular Electronics showed the Altair 8800, a build-it-yourself computer kit from MITS in Albuquerque, based on Intel's 8080 chip. It had switches and blinking lights instead of a keyboard and screen. Two young fans, Bill Gates and Paul Allen, wrote a BASIC interpreter for it, which became the first product of their new company, Microsoft.
items.q: Which processor powered the Altair 8800?
items.a: The Intel 8080.

items.title: Keep a low-energy menu
items.body: Some hours the brain is a sports car, some hours it's a bicycle with a flat. Write a short list of useful tasks that need almost no willpower: sort the downloads folder, water the plants, rename files, refill the stapler. When energy dips, pick from the menu instead of forcing the hard thing or scrolling. It's still progress.
items.hook: Wonder: what three tasks would go on your low-energy menu?

items.title: AT&T runs about 500 agent workflows in production
items.body: AT&T says its Business Agent Foundry now runs close to 500 agentic workflows in production, handling over a million transactions a month and about 45 billion tokens a day. Uses include customer provisioning, network operations and sales prospecting, and it plans to triple the count within a year. These are the company's own figures.
items.hook: Wonder: which boring, repeatable task in your week would make a good first agent workflow?

items.title: 'Serendipity' came from Sri Lanka's old name
items.body: In 1754 the writer Horace Walpole coined 'serendipity' in a letter, inspired by a tale called The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept discovering things they weren't looking for. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka. So the word for happy accidents is a little souvenir from an island just south of Tamil Nadu.
items.q: Which country's old name is hidden in 'serendipity'?
items.a: Sri Lanka (Serendip).

items.title: Hick's law: more choices, slower start
items.body: In the early 1950s William Hick and Ray Hyman found that the time people take to choose grows with the number of options, roughly with its logarithm. Doubling the options adds about the same small delay each time. It's why a short menu feels fast. When you're stuck, try trimming the choices before trying harder.
items.hook: Wonder: which daily choice could you shrink to two options?

items.title: The Ashtadiggajas: eight poets, eight elephants
items.body: Krishnadevaraya, who ruled Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529, gathered eight celebrated Telugu poets at his court. They were called the Ashtadiggajas, after the eight mythical elephants said to hold up the eight directions of the world. Allasani Peddana, honoured as the 'grandfather of Telugu poetry', was among them, and later tradition counts the witty Tenali Ramakrishna too. The king was a poet himself.
items.q: Why were Krishnadevaraya's eight court poets called the Ashtadiggajas?
items.a: After the eight mythical elephants that hold up the eight directions.

items.title: Nakamura's 74th Bullet Brawl
items.body: Hikaru Nakamura won Saturday's Bullet Brawl on Chess.com with 178 points, 21 clear of Jeffery Xiong. It's his 74th Bullet Brawl title and his 25th of 2026 alone. IM Renato Terry was third, and WIM Melika Mohammadi took the women's prize. The next Brawl is on 21 November.
items.hook: Wonder: what does one-minute chess train that slow chess can't?

items.title: CQRS: one model to write, another to read
items.body: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits a system's writes from its reads. Commands go to a model shaped for rules and consistency; queries hit read models shaped for the screens that need them, often denormalised copies kept up to date from events. It shines when reads and writes look very different, and it's overkill for a simple CRUD app, because you now own the job of keeping the read side in sync.
items.q: What new job does CQRS give you in exchange for tailored read models?
items.a: Keeping the read models in sync with the write side (usually eventually consistent).

items.title: Monday, the water tank
items.body:
Up on the roof the tank is filling,
a low hum like someone thinking.
The day's dishes are drying in a row,
each one a small finished thing.
Down the lane a scooter coughs, then settles.
The week has started.
That was the hard part,
and it's done.

items.title: Euclid finds its first comet
items.body: ESA's Euclid telescope, built to map dark matter, has discovered its first comet: C/2026 S1 (Euclid), about 1.3 billion km away, between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. Mikko Pöntinen of the University of Helsinki spotted it as a small streak across five sets of images from September. A fuzzy glow around it hints that it's already shedding dust and gas.
items.q: Between which two planets' orbits was Euclid's first comet found?
items.a: Jupiter and Saturn.

A companion agent can act on the notes afterwards, for example by drafting the follow-up email. It's a preview for now, so details may change.

items.a: Act on them, for example drafting a follow-up email.

items.title: Ask the agent where it's unsure
items.body: At the end of a task, add one line to your prompt: 'List anything you assumed or weren't sure about.' Agents often make reasonable guesses silently. Getting them written down turns hidden guesses into a short checklist you can review in a minute.
items.hook: Wonder: which of your own assumptions today would you want written down?

items.title: Venus is the planets' only goddess
items.body: Of the eight planets, Venus is the only one named after a female figure from mythology, the Roman goddess of love. Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are named for male gods, and Earth's name comes from old English and Germanic words for the ground. Venus's surface features make up for it: almost all are named after women.
items.hook: Wonder: if you could name a crater on Venus, who would it honour?

items.title: Whoever says it
items.body: Whatever is said, and whoever says it, wisdom looks past the speaker to the truth of the words.

items.title: Outposts: a home your knight can keep
items.body: An outpost is a square in your opponent's half that no enemy pawn can ever attack, ideally backed by one of your own pawns. A knight planted there is very hard to remove; it can only be traded off by a minor piece. When you look at a position, ask: which squares can the opponent's pawns no longer guard?
items.q: What makes a square an outpost?
items.a: No enemy pawn can attack it, and ideally your own pawn supports it.

items.title: India's first digital computer arrived in Kolkata
items.body: In 1956 the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata installed an HEC-2M, a British-made machine, usually counted as the first digital computer in India. The ISI, founded by P. C. Mahalanobis, needed it for heavy statistical work, and it became a training ground for some of India's earliest programmers.
items.hook: Wonder: what problem would you have queued up for India's only computer in 1956?

items.title: Mahamaham, the festival on Jupiter's clock
items.body: At Kumbakonam, the Mahamaham festival is held about once every twelve years, when Jupiter enters the sign of Leo (Simha). Pilgrims gather to bathe in the Mahamaham tank, surrounded by small shrines. Because Jupiter takes close to twelve years to circle the Sun, an ancient festival calendar is quietly keeping time with a planet. The last one was in 2016.
items.q: Roughly how often is the Mahamaham festival held, and why?
items.a: About every 12 years, when Jupiter enters Leo (Simha).

items.title: Let an object carry the feeling
items.body: Instead of telling us a character is lonely, show what they do with an object: setting two cups out by habit, then putting one back. Readers trust what they notice more than what they're told. Pick one small thing in the scene and let it quietly hold the emotion.
items.hook: Wonder: what object in your room would tell a stranger how your week is going?

items.title: Apollo 12 landed next to an old friend
items.body: Apollo 12 launched on 14 November 1969 and touched down five days later in the Ocean of Storms, close enough to the robotic Surveyor 3 lander (there since 1967) for Pete Conrad and Alan Bean to walk over to it. They brought pieces of Surveyor home, including its TV camera, so engineers could study how materials had fared after two and a half years on the Moon. It was a showcase of pinpoint landing.
items.q: Which earlier spacecraft did Apollo 12's astronauts visit on the Moon?
items.a: Surveyor 3, which had landed in 1967.

items.title: Building agents in Java with Bedrock and Spring AI
items.body: A new AWS blog post walks Java developers through building autonomous agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI. It covers the parts that matter in production: tool calling, memory, resilience and coordinating several agents together. Handy if you'd like to try agents without leaving the Spring world.
items.q: Which Java framework does the AWS guide pair with Bedrock?
items.a: Spring AI.

items.title: Make Monday's first task tiny
items.body: The start of a week can feel like a cliff. Choose a first task so small it's almost silly: open the document, reply to one message, fill one water bottle. Finishing something in the first ten minutes sets the tone, and momentum is easier to keep than to find.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the smallest real thing you could finish in the next ten minutes?

items.title: Incubation: step away from the puzzle
items.body: Stuck on a problem? A break can help. A 2009 meta-analysis by Ut Na Sio and Thomas Ormerod found an 'incubation effect': setting a problem aside often improved later solutions, especially for creative problems and when the break was filled with a light, undemanding activity. Work on it properly first, then walk away and let it sit.
items.q: According to the incubation research, what kind of break helps most?
items.a: One filled with a light, undemanding activity, after real work on the problem first.

items.title: Cheetahs purr, but can't roar
items.body: Big cats split roughly into roarers and purrers. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars can roar; cheetahs can't, but they purr steadily, much like a house cat, and also make high bird-like chirps to call to each other.
items.q: What sound do cheetahs make instead of roaring?
items.a: They purr, and they chirp.

items.title: Read-your-writes consistency
items.body: You update your profile photo, refresh, and see the old one. Infuriating, even if the system is 'eventually consistent'. Read-your-writes is the small promise that fixes it: a user always sees their own latest changes. Common ways to keep it: route that user's reads to the leader for a short while after a write, or attach the write's version to their session and only read from replicas that have caught up to it.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your system could a user be surprised by their own old data?

items.title: Pavithra R V is a world amateur champion
items.body: The FIDE World Amateur Championships finished in Klang, Malaysia, with six titles across rating bands. India's Pavithra R V won the Women's Under-2300 section unbeaten, on 7.5 out of 9. The highest score of the event belonged to Mongolia's Javkhlan Bayarjargal, who won the Open Under-1700 with 8.5/9.
items.q: Which section did Pavithra R V win in Klang?
items.a: Women's Under-2300, unbeaten on 7.5/9.

items.title: The key cutter's spare
items.body: The key cutter under the banyan tree made two copies for every customer and gave back only one. People assumed he forgot. When old Mrs. Iyer locked herself out on a rainy night, he walked over with an umbrella, found her key on the board behind his stool, and opened her door without a word. 'Everyone loses one key in their life,' he said, handing it over. 'I just keep it until then.'

items.title: Euclid shares its first big data release
items.body: ESA's Euclid space telescope has released its first large batch of survey data. Euclid is building a 3D map of the Universe, using a 600-megapixel visible-light camera alongside an infrared instrument, to learn how dark matter and dark energy have shaped the cosmos. This release is an early stepping stone toward that full map.
items.hook: Wonder: how do you map the third dimension of the sky, when every galaxy looks flat?

items.title: Salesforce opens up a speech-to-text model
items.body: Salesforce has released SOV-Transcribe-1 with open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. It's a non-streaming transcription model covering seven languages, and you can steer it with plain-language instructions, for example formatting preferences or hints about unusual vocabulary. Organisations can run it on their own machines. The benchmark figures so far are Salesforce's own.
items.q: Under what licence is SOV-Transcribe-1 released?
items.a: Apache 2.0, with open weights.

items.title: By degrees
items.body: How poor are they that have not patience! What wound did ever heal but by degrees?

items.title: Zuse's Z3, built from relays
items.body: In 1941 in Berlin, Konrad Zuse completed the Z3, widely regarded as the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. It used about 2,600 telephone relays, worked in binary and even used floating-point numbers. Programs were read from punched film. A faithful reconstruction can be seen today at the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
items.q: What switching parts did the Z3 use?
items.a: Electromechanical telephone relays, about 2,600 of them.

items.title: Curiosity opens the memory door
items.body: In a 2014 study by Matthias Gruber, Bernard Gelman and Charan Ranganath, people rated how curious they were about trivia questions. They remembered answers to the questions they were curious about better, and even remembered unrelated faces shown while they waited for those answers. A good question before a lesson isn't decoration; it prepares the ground.
items.hook: Wonder: what question could you ask yourself before you start today's reading?

items.title: 'Catamaran' is a Tamil word
items.body: The English word 'catamaran' comes from the Tamil kattumaram, roughly 'tied wood': a raft of logs lashed together, still used by fishers along the Coromandel coast. English borrowed it in the 1600s, and today it also names sleek twin-hulled sailing boats.
items.hook: Wonder: what other everyday English words started in Tamil?

items.title: Thambiran Vanakkam, 1578
items.body: Thambiran Vanakkam, a short Tamil Christian prayer book printed in Kollam (Quilon) in 1578, is generally counted as the first book printed in an Indian language. Its Tamil letters were cut as metal type by Portuguese Jesuits, with Henrique Henriques among those behind it. A small book, and the start of a long story for Tamil in print.
items.q: In which script was the first book printed in an Indian language set?
items.a: Tamil, in Thambiran Vanakkam (Kollam, 1578).

items.title: Java 21: Math.clamp
items.body: Keeping a number inside a range used to mean Math.max(min, Math.min(max, value)), which is easy to get backwards. Since Java 21 you can write Math.clamp(value, 0, 100). There are overloads for int, long, float and double, and it throws if min is greater than max, so a swapped range gets caught instead of quietly misbehaving.
items.q: What does Math.clamp(150, 0, 100) return?
items.a: 100. Values above the range are pulled down to max.

items.title: Guess, then time it
items.body: Before a small task, write your guess for how long it'll take. Then time it. No judging, just two numbers side by side. After a week you'll know your personal multiplier (many people find their guesses run short), and planning gets kinder because it's built on what actually happens.
items.hook: Wonder: which everyday task do you most often underestimate?

items.title: Total Chess: the final four are set
items.body: The group stage of the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot in Budapest has finished. The group winners are Alireza Firouzja, Fabiano Caruana, Anish Giri and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave. The semifinals pair Vachier-Lagrave with Giri and Caruana with Firouzja. In Group D, Vaishali Rameshbabu's last-round win over Arjun Erigaisi helped settle first place for MVL. The knockout stage begins on Tuesday, 17 November.
items.q: Who are the four Total Chess semifinalists?
items.a: Firouzja, Caruana, Giri and Vachier-Lagrave.

items.title: Monday, the gate latch
items.body:
The gate latch clicks the week open.
A neighbour's broom says good morning to the road,
the milk van hums its one tune,
and the sky, not yet decided,
keeps a little grey for later.
No hurry. The day has only just
put its shoes on.

items.title: LOFAR's deepest look at the low-frequency radio sky
items.body: An international team led by Leiden University has used the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), a network of radio antennas spread across Europe, to make what it describes as the sharpest and most sensitive image yet of the sky at low radio frequencies. At these long wavelengths, the sky shows things visible light can't: the radio glow of distant galaxies and the jets streaming from their black holes.
items.q: Which radio telescope network made the new deepest low-frequency sky image?
items.a: LOFAR, the Low Frequency Array, in a Leiden-led study.

items.title: Folio: agent summaries that keep a way back to the evidence
items.body: A new preprint describes Folio, a way for long-running agents to shrink old history without losing the trail. Alongside short model-written notes, it keeps a manifest of runtime events and the captured source records, each with a stable handle, so the agent can reopen the exact detail later. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks it reported 66 successes, against 54 for plain model-written compaction on the same setup. The authors' test used one model and one benchmark, so it's an early result.
items.hook: Wonder: when you summarise your own notes, do you keep a pointer back to the original?

items.title: Filter, refilled
items.body:
The decoction drips through the night,
one patient brown bead at a time.
No one is watching.
That's how the best things are made:
slowly, in the dark,
ready by morning.

items.title: There's a word for winter sun: apricity
items.body: 'Apricity' means the warmth of the sun in winter. It appears in Henry Cockeram's English dictionary of 1623 and then mostly vanished from use, but it's a lovely word to have for that first sunny patch on a cold morning.
items.q: What does 'apricity' mean?
items.a: The warmth of the sun in winter.

items.title: Count-min sketch: counting in a small box
items.body: To count how often millions of different items appear, without a giant map, keep a small grid of counters: a few rows, each with its own hash function. For each item, bump one counter per row. To estimate a count, take the smallest of its counters. Collisions can only add, never subtract, so the answer may run a little high but never low.
items.hook: Wonder: where would 'never too low, sometimes a bit high' be good enough for you?

items.title: Think of their virtues
items.body: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee.

items.title: The desperado
items.body: When one of your pieces is going to be captured anyway, it can become a desperado: before it goes, it grabs whatever it can, often with check or with a capture of its own. Before you recapture automatically, check whether the opponent's doomed piece can take something first, and whether yours can.
items.q: What's a desperado in chess?
items.a: A piece that's lost anyway and grabs as much material as it can before it's taken.

items.title: The first 'software' in print
items.body: The statistician John Tukey is credited with the earliest known published use of 'software' in the computing sense, in a 1958 article in the American Mathematical Monthly. He contrasted it with the 'hardware' of tubes, transistors and wires. A decade earlier he had also coined 'bit'.
items.hook: Wonder: which everyday tech word of today will sound quaint in sixty years?

items.title: Let the agent fetch tools, not carry them all
items.body: Giving an agent every tool description up front fills its context and blurs its choices. A calmer pattern: keep a short core set always visible, and let the agent search a catalogue for anything else when it needs it. It's how a good workshop works: a few tools on the bench, the rest labelled on the wall.
items.q: What's the downside of loading every tool description into an agent's context at once?
items.a: It fills the context and makes choosing the right tool harder.

items.title: Name things the way your character would
items.body: A botanist sees 'a neem, a tamarind, two gulmohars'; a tired commuter sees 'trees'. The words you use for objects quietly tell the reader whose eyes we're behind. In a close point of view, let the nouns come from the character's own knowledge, job and mood, and you'll rarely need to say what they're feeling.

items.title: Andromeda is wider than six full Moons
items.body: To the naked eye, the Andromeda Galaxy is just a faint oval smudge, because you only see its bright core. Long-exposure photos reveal its full disc stretching about three degrees across the sky, roughly six times the width of the full Moon. If its outer glow were bright enough to see, it would be one of the largest things in the night sky.
items.hook: Wonder: what else is up there, large but too faint to notice?

items.title: Owls can't move their eyes
items.body: An owl's large eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets, so it can't roll them to glance sideways. Instead it turns its whole head, as far as about 270 degrees, thanks to extra neck vertebrae and blood vessels arranged to keep flowing while it twists.
items.q: Why does an owl turn its head so far?
items.a: Its tube-shaped eyes are fixed in their sockets and can't move.

items.title: Srirangam's gopuram, finished centuries later
items.body: The base of the great southern gateway tower at Srirangam's Ranganathaswamy Temple was begun centuries ago and then left unfinished. It was completed only in 1987, rising in 13 tiers to about 73 metres, making it one of the tallest temple towers in Asia. Generations walked past a gateway waiting to be finished.
items.hook: Wonder: what's something you started that could still be finished, slowly?

items.title: The mere-exposure effect
items.body: In studies going back to Robert Zajonc in 1968, people tend to like things more simply because they've seen them before: unfamiliar words, faces, shapes, tunes. The effect is gentle and fades if repetition turns into overload. It's one reason a new piece of music or a new habit often feels better on the fifth try than the first.
items.q: What's the mere-exposure effect?
items.a: We tend to like things more just because we've encountered them before.

items.title: Keep supplies where the task happens
items.body: If the scissors live in the kitchen but parcels get opened in the hallway, every parcel becomes a small expedition. Buy a second cheap pair, a spare charger, an extra pen, and keep each one where the job actually happens. Removing one walk across the house removes one chance to get sidetracked.
items.hook: Wonder: which object do you most often walk to fetch?

items.title: The fortress
items.body: Sometimes the side with less material can build a position the stronger side simply cannot break: the king guards the entry squares, a piece covers the rest, and no pawn can make progress. That's a fortress. When you're worse, ask not 'how do I win this back?' but 'is there a setup where nothing gets in?' Many lost-looking endgames are saved this way.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a fortress look like in a busy week?

items.title: Tail latency grows with fan-out
items.body: If a single server answers slowly 1% of the time, that sounds fine. But a request that fans out to 100 servers has to wait for the slowest one: the chance that at least one is slow is 1 − 0.99^100, about 63%. That's why large systems obsess over the 99th percentile, and why Jeff Dean and Luiz Barroso's 2013 'The Tail at Scale' recommends hedged and tied requests.
items.q: With a 1% slow rate per server, about how often does a 100-way fan-out hit at least one slow server?
items.a: About 63% of the time (1 − 0.99^100).

items.title: The bangle seller's spare
items.body: Every evening at the temple steps, the bangle seller kept one glass bangle off the stick: a plain green, slightly too big for anyone. Children asked about it; she said it was for later. Tonight a small girl came with her grandmother, whose wrist had grown thin. The green one slid on and stayed. 'Later,' the seller said, and began threading a new spare.

items.title: Plain keyword search keeps up at picking tools
items.body: A community analysis published on Towards Data Science tested how agents find the right tool from a large catalogue. On a 200-question slice of the ToolRet benchmark, classic BM25 keyword search tied an 8-billion-parameter embedding model while running about 40 times faster on a CPU. Both did worse as the tool pool grew, a reminder that well-described tools matter more than fancy retrieval.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your own stack might a simple method quietly match a heavy one?

items.title: Gemini XII, sixty years on
items.body: From 11 to 15 November 1966, Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin flew Gemini XII, the last mission of the Gemini programme. Earlier spacewalks had left astronauts exhausted. Aldrin, who had rehearsed underwater, used handholds, foot restraints and frequent rests, and spent about five and a half hours working outside the capsule across three outings. It showed that careful, unhurried work in space was possible, just in time for Apollo.
items.q: What helped Aldrin's Gemini XII spacewalks succeed where earlier ones had tired astronauts out?
items.a: Underwater rehearsal, handholds and foot restraints, and planned rests.

items.title: Aim high anyway
items.body: Let every thought you think be a thought of rising. Even if the aim falls short, the aiming is never wasted.

items.title: Hollerith's census cards
items.body: The 1880 US census took most of a decade to tabulate by hand. For 1890, Herman Hollerith's electric tabulator read punched cards, one per person: a pin passing through a hole closed a circuit and moved a counter dial. The count went far faster. Hollerith's company later merged into the firm that, in 1924, renamed itself IBM.
items.q: How did Hollerith's tabulator 'read' a punched card?
items.a: Pins passed through the holes and closed electric circuits, each advancing a counter.

items.title: The narwhal's tusk is a tooth
items.body: A narwhal's long, spiralled tusk is not a horn: it's a canine tooth, usually the left one, that grows straight out through the upper lip. It can reach around three metres, and it twists in a left-handed spiral as it grows. Most tusked narwhals are males, though a few females grow one too.
items.hook: Wonder: why might a tooth grow in a spiral rather than straight?

items.title: Change blindness
items.body: In a 1998 study by Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin, a researcher stopped passers-by to ask for directions. Midway through, two workers carried a door between them, and the researcher was swapped for a different person. About half the people giving directions didn't notice. We see far less detail than it feels like we do; attention, not the eyes, decides what gets stored.
items.q: In the 'door study', roughly what share of people failed to notice they were talking to a new person?
items.a: About half.

items.title: Giri takes the lead in Group C
items.body: On the penultimate day of the Total Chess pilot in Budapest, Anish Giri beat Abhimanyu Mishra to move to the top of Group C. In Group D, Arjun Erigaisi beat Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, leaving Vachier-Lagrave, Hans Niemann and Erigaisi level at the top, while Alireza Firouzja still leads Group A. Only the four group winners go through to the knockout, so Sunday's final round settles it.
items.hook: Wonder: how differently would you play knowing only first place in your group counts?

items.title: Thanjavur paintings glow with real gold
items.body: The Thanjavur style of painting flourished under the Nayak and later Maratha rulers of Thanjavur, roughly from the 17th to the 19th century. Artists built up raised relief with a chalk-and-gum paste, then laid thin gold foil over it, so haloes and jewellery catch the light. Some panels are also set with glass beads or stones, and the deep reds, greens and blues around them make the gold seem to float.
items.q: What gives Thanjavur paintings their raised, glowing details?
items.a: A built-up chalk-and-gum relief covered with thin gold foil, sometimes set with beads or stones.

items.title: Claude helps read Gödel's shorthand notebooks
items.body: Logician Jan von Plato told The Guardian that Claude worked through Kurt Gödel's 1,009 pages of notes, written in the old Gabelsberger shorthand, in a couple of days this autumn. The reading surfaced hundreds of proved results that had never been catalogued, reported as 663 theorems. Scholars still check each one; the AI's job was to make a near-unreadable archive searchable.
items.hook: Wonder: what other notebooks are waiting, unread, in a script few people can still decipher?

items.title: Sunday, 10 pm
items.body:
The week is folded on the chair,
its sleeves still holding the shape of my arms.
The kitchen tap lets go one drop,
then thinks better of the next.
Somewhere a scooter takes the long way home.
I leave the window open a finger's width
so tomorrow can find its way in quietly.

items.title: Java: Arrays.asList is fixed-size
items.body: Arrays.asList(a, b, c) gives you a list that is a thin view over an array. You can set() an element (and it writes through to the array), but add() or remove() throws UnsupportedOperationException. If you need a growable list, wrap it: new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(...)). If you want a fully unchangeable one, List.of(...) is clearer, and it rejects nulls.
items.q: What happens if you call add() on the list returned by Arrays.asList?
items.a: It throws UnsupportedOperationException, because the list is fixed-size.

items.title: Turn off the badges
items.body: Those little red number bubbles on app icons are designed to tug at you, and each tug costs a moment of attention. Go through your phone once and switch off badges for everything except the two or three apps where a count really matters. The apps still work; they just stop calling your name.
items.hook: Wonder: which single badge do you check most without needing to?

items.title: Euclid finds the most distant quasars yet
items.body: ESA's Euclid telescope has turned up 31 quasars from the early universe, 12 of them at redshift 7 or beyond. Two set new distance records, at redshifts 7.77 and 7.69, edging past the previous record of 7.64 from 2021. Each was already shining as brightly as about a trillion Suns when the universe was roughly 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.
items.q: Roughly how old was the universe when the light from Euclid's record quasars set out?
items.a: About 670 million years old, around 5% of its current age.

items.title: Sea otters keep a favourite rock
items.body: Sea otters use stones to crack open shellfish, floating on their backs and banging the shell against a rock on their chest. Many keep a favourite stone tucked in the loose skin pouch under a forearm and carry it from dive to dive.
items.hook: Wonder: what's your own favourite, well-worn tool?

items.title: Name the tools the way you'd name them for a new colleague
items.body: Agents choose tools largely from their names and descriptions. 'search_orders_by_customer_email' gets picked correctly far more often than 'query2'. Write each tool's name and one-line description as if handing it to a new teammate on day one: what it does, when to use it, and what it returns.
items.hook: Wonder: would a new teammate understand your tool names without asking?

items.title: The Immortal Game
items.body: In London in 1851, Adolf Anderssen sacrificed a bishop, both rooks and then his queen against Lionel Kieseritzky, and still delivered checkmate with his three remaining minor pieces. It was a casual game, played between sessions of a tournament, yet it's still taught as a celebration of daring, open play.
items.q: Which pieces did Anderssen give up in the Immortal Game?
items.a: A bishop, both rooks and his queen.

items.title: Give the scene a weather of its own
items.body: Weather in a story doesn't need to mirror the mood. A quarrel in bright, cheerful sunshine, or good news on a dull, drizzly afternoon, can feel truer and more surprising than a storm on cue. Choose the weather, then let your character notice it once, in their own words.
items.hook: Wonder: what's the least likely weather for the scene you're writing?

items.title: Pipes began as a garden-hose memo
items.body: In a 1964 memo Doug McIlroy wrote that programs should connect like segments of garden hose, so the output of one could screw into the next. The idea waited until 1973, when Ken Thompson added pipes to Unix in a single night of work. The humble | still lets small tools team up into big jobs.
items.hook: Wonder: which two small tools in your day could be joined like hose?

items.title: Bluebirds aren't blue inside
items.body: Most birds can't make blue pigment. A bluebird's or blue jay's feathers contain tiny structures that scatter blue light back at your eye. Crush a blue feather and the colour vanishes into brown-grey, because the structure, not a dye, made the blue.
items.q: Why does a crushed blue feather lose its colour?
items.a: The blue comes from the feather's microscopic structure, not pigment.

items.title: Mariner 9, the first Mars orbiter
items.body: In November 1971 NASA's Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. It arrived during a global dust storm and simply waited for the dust to settle. When the air cleared, it mapped most of Mars and revealed giant volcanoes and the vast canyon system now called Valles Marineris, named after the spacecraft.
items.hook: Wonder: what would you photograph first if you'd waited months for the dust to clear?

items.title: Madurai's towers of colour
items.body: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai has 14 gopurams, its tall gateway towers, crowded with thousands of painted figures of gods, animals and guardians. Much of the complex we see today was built or rebuilt under the Nayak rulers in the 16th and 17th centuries, and the tallest tower, on the south side, rises about 50 metres.
items.q: How many gopurams does the Meenakshi Amman Temple have?
items.a: Fourteen.

items.title: The frequency illusion
items.body: Learn a new word or notice a new car model, and suddenly it seems to be everywhere. It isn't more common; your attention has a new filter, and memory pays extra attention when the new thing turns up. Learners can use it on purpose: name a concept clearly and you'll start spotting it in the wild.
items.hook: Wonder: what idea from this feed might you start noticing everywhere this week?

items.title: Java 9: Stream.iterate with a stop sign
items.body: The three-argument Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) works like a for loop as a stream: Stream.iterate(1, x -> x < 1000, x -> x * 2) gives 1, 2, 4 … 512 and then stops. No limit() guessing, and no infinite stream by accident.
items.q: What are the three arguments to Stream.iterate in Java 9+?
items.a: A seed, a condition to keep going, and a step function.

items.title: Not in our stars
items.body:
The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars,
But in ourselves.
items.hook: Wonder: what small thing is already within your reach today?

items.title: The lost-and-found shelf
items.body: At the small station, the stationmaster kept a lost-and-found shelf: one glove, a tiffin box, a child's blue pencil. Every Sunday he dusted them and set them a little straighter. Nobody ever came for the glove. But one morning a girl stepped off the 7:10, walked straight to the shelf, and took the pencil. 'I drew the river with it,' she said, 'and it wasn't finished.' He nodded as if he'd been expecting her all year.

items.title: OpenAI and Databricks lay out the playbook
items.body: Databricks published a guide to its partnership with OpenAI, describing three common ways companies use the pair: ChatGPT with a Databricks Genie plugin for business users, Codex routed through Databricks' gateway for engineers, and custom agents built on GPT models. The idea is that AI works on a company's governed data without that data needing to leave its guarded home.

items.title: Batch errands by place, not by list
items.body: A long errand list feels like ten separate efforts. Group the items by where they happen ('near the bank', 'at home on the phone', 'online'), then do one place at a time. Every switch between places costs energy, so fewer switches leaves more for the errands themselves.
items.q: Why group errands by location?
items.a: It cuts the number of switches, and each switch costs energy.

items.title: The minority attack
items.body: In some Queen's Gambit structures, White has two pawns on the queenside against Black's three. Oddly, White pushes those fewer pawns forward (b4–b5) to swap them off and leave Black with a weak, isolated or backward pawn on c6 or d5. The smaller group attacks the bigger one to create a long-term target.
items.hook: Wonder: when does having fewer pawns on a wing make attacking easier?

items.title: Sketchpad, drawing with light
items.body: In 1963 Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad for his MIT PhD. With a light pen on a screen, you could draw lines and circles, copy shapes, and add constraints like 'keep these lines parallel'. It introduced ideas we now take for granted (objects and instances, zooming, direct manipulation) and is often called the ancestor of graphical interfaces and CAD.
items.q: What input device did Sketchpad use?
items.a: A light pen.

items.title: Endeavour's new home opens
items.body: California's new Air & Space Center in Los Angeles, the home of space shuttle Endeavour, opened to visitors on 13 November. Endeavour flew 25 missions before retiring in 2011, and in its new gallery it is displayed upright, ready-for-launch style, with its external tank and boosters.
items.hook: Wonder: how does a 37-metre spacecraft feel when you stand beneath it?

items.title: Java 15: String.formatted
items.body: Instead of String.format("Hi %s, you have %d items", name, n), you can write "Hi %s, you have %d items".formatted(name, n). Same format rules, but it reads left to right and chains nicely, especially after a text block.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your code does a format string hide at the end of a long line?

items.title: 'Nice' used to mean foolish
items.body: The word 'nice' comes through Old French from Latin nescius, 'not knowing'. In medieval English it meant silly or ignorant. Over the centuries it drifted to 'fussy', then 'precise' (a 'nice distinction'), and only later to 'pleasant'.
items.q: What did the Latin root of 'nice' mean?
items.a: 'Not knowing' (nescius).

items.title: The Kural reaches English readers
items.body: In 1886 the missionary scholar G. U. Pope published an English translation of the Thirukkural, Thiruvalluvar's 1,330 couplets. He spent decades in Tamil Nadu and grew so fond of the language that he asked to be remembered as a student of Tamil. His translation helped carry the Kural's quiet, practical wisdom to readers far beyond the Tamil country.
items.hook: Wonder: which couplet would you choose to carry into another language?

items.title: llama.cpp reaches version 1.0
items.body: The team behind llama.cpp, the popular engine for running language models on ordinary computers, released v1.0.0 of both llama.cpp and its ggml library on 13 November. The new version numbers follow semantic versioning: a major bump now signals a breaking change to the public C API, minor bumps add features or models, and patches fix bugs. The project is about three and a half years old and supports more than 150 model architecture variants.
items.q: In llama.cpp's new scheme, what does a major version bump signal?
items.a: A breaking change to its public C API.

items.title: Vary the practice
items.body: Practising one exact version of a skill feels smooth, but practising small variations often transfers better. Children who practised beanbag throws at two distances did well at a third distance they'd never tried. Change the angle, the example, the wording, and your brain learns the rule underneath rather than one groove.
items.hook: Wonder: what's one small variation you could add to something you practise?

items.title: Sunday, the slow gate
items.body:
The gate creaks once
and then decides
to stay half open.

A neighbour's radio,
low, somewhere.
The dosa pan, warming.

No one is late today.
Even the crows
are taking their time.

items.title: Hot keys and salted keys
items.body: Sharding spreads data by key, but one popular key (a celebrity's post, a big customer) can still pin a single shard at 100%. One fix is salting: write to key#0 … key#9 chosen at random, so the load lands on ten shards. The price is on the read side: you now read all ten and combine them. Salt only the keys that are truly hot.
items.q: What does 'salting' a hot key trade away?
items.a: Cheaper reads: you must read and merge all the salted copies.

items.title: Cramling and Strutinskaya crowned senior champions
items.body: The FIDE World Senior Championships finished in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia, on 14 November, with 385 players from 65 countries. Pia Cramling won Women 50+ with 9/11, and Galina Strutinskaya took Women 65+ with an outstanding 10/11. Murtas Kazhgaleyev won Open 50+ on 8.5/11, and Zurab Sturua topped a three-way tie on 8.5/11 in Open 65+, ahead of Keith Arkell and Alexander Mikhalevski.
items.q: Who won the Women 65+ title, and with what score?
items.a: Galina Strutinskaya, 10/11.

items.title: One tab in, one tab out
items.body: Open browser tabs quietly pile up as unfinished promises. Try a simple rule while you work: before opening a new tab, close one you're done with. If a tab still matters, drop its link into a 'later' note so closing it doesn't feel like losing it.
items.hook: Wonder: how many of your open tabs are really reminders in disguise?

items.title: The night it rained meteors
items.body: On 17 November 1966, observers in the western United States saw the Leonids turn into a true meteor storm, with peak rates estimated at around 144,000 meteors an hour, dozens every second for a short while. Storms like that happen when Earth passes through an unusually dense, fresh trail of dust left by Comet Tempel–Tuttle. In an ordinary year the Leonids give a calm handful an hour, and that's still lovely.
items.q: Which comet leaves the dust that becomes the Leonids?
items.a: Comet Tempel–Tuttle.

items.title: Friendship's real work
items.body: Friendship is not for laughing together. It is for stepping in, firmly, when a friend begins to stray.

items.title: Cloudflare open-sources Kitesurf
items.body: Cloudflare has released Kitesurf, its experimental browser engine built for AI agents, as open source. Kitesurf runs inside lightweight V8 isolates on Cloudflare Workers rather than as a full desktop browser. Now anyone can read the code, run it locally, or deploy their own copy to their Workers account.
items.hook: Wonder: what does a browser look like when nobody needs to see the pixels?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body: Try answering before you peek. Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than re-reading does.
items.q: 1) What does the Java 22 underscore mean? 2) Which project now hosts the Agent Name Service? 3) What are Titan's lakes made of?
items.a: 1) An unnamed variable you deliberately don't use. 2) The Linux Foundation. 3) Liquid methane and ethane.

items.title: Ledger, Saturday night
items.body:
Two letters answered.
One plant watered twice by mistake.
A long call with an old friend.
Nothing finished, nothing lost.
I'll call it a fair day.

items.title: Cats can't taste sweet
items.body: Cats lack a working sweet-taste receptor: one of the two genes needed for it is broken in cats, as researchers reported in 2005. As strict meat-eaters they never needed it, so a cat ignoring cake isn't fussiness.
items.q: Why don't cats care about sweet food?
items.a: A gene needed for the sweet-taste receptor doesn't work in cats.

items.title: LangChain raises a Series C
items.body: LangChain, maker of the LangChain framework and the LangSmith platform for testing and watching agents, raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation, led by CapitalG. The company says LangSmith now has about 7,000 customers.
items.hook: Wonder: why do agent teams need a place to watch traces, not just a framework?
